title: 'I'm responsible for winning in the future': How SA Rugby is preparing for life after Rassie
article_text:
Cut off the head of the snake and the body will die, or so the old adage goes. After Rassie Erasmus received a six-match ban, South African rugby has an opportunity to demonstrate its success is not entirely dependent on the brilliance of one man.

Whatever the outcome of this turbulent November, the Springboks will one day have to contemplate a future without their talismanic coach, who is contracted until the end of the 2031 World Cup. His greatest legacy might be to leave behind a system capable of sustaining the success he has engineered.

“Rassie’s responsible for winning today, and I’m responsible for winning in the future,” explains SA Rugby’s general manager of high performance.

Succession planning extends beyond identifying the next generation of Springboks. Physiotherapists, doctors, conditioning specialists, team managers and coaches are being prepared for positions that might only become available several years from now.

Until recently, those working with South Africa’s various national teams operated largely in isolation from their counterparts. Wessels has brought people with similar jobs together, regardless of which team they serve. A solution to a problem encountered by the sevens coaches might now benefit the Junior Springboks or women’s side.

“We don’t necessarily want a revolution one day in the Springbok team,” Wessels says. “We simply want evolution.”

But where does South Africa find its coaches? Wessels’s own career provides some answers. His first assignment was coaching the under-nine Cs at Reddam House primary school in Cape Town, an experience more akin to babysitting than coaching rugby. There he encountered Les Kiss, the current Wallabies head coach, who was then working with the Springboks and ran sessions at the school as a favour to the headmaster.

Some of the best coaches in the country are actually coaching at school level. You really are coaching against really world-class coaches, many of whom have got senior franchise experience.

“I just remember thinking, geez, I’ve never seen someone talk about rugby like this,” Wessels recalls.

After spending time with Kiss in Australia, Wessels applied for a coaching position at Bishops, one of South Africa’s most prestigious rugby schools, but was rejected. He travelled two minutes down the road to Rondebosch Boys’ High, requesting an apprenticeship alongside former Springbok hooker Shaun Povey. Together they coached the under-16 As before graduating to the first XV.

A presentation to schoolmasters brought Wessels into contact with Erasmus, then in charge of the Stormers. Armed with his phone number, Wessels persistently badgered him until he was offered work with Western Province and subsequently the Stormers.

Wessels also coached at the University of Cape Town before joining Jake White’s Brumbies as a defensive consultant. In 2016, aged 33, he became the youngest head coach in Super Rugby history when appointed by the Western Force. He subsequently guided the Melbourne Rebels to their first finals appearance in Super Rugby AU in 2020 before returning to South Africa in 2022.

“Some of the best coaches in the country are actually coaching at [school] level,” Wessels says. “You really are coaching against really world-class coaches, many of whom have got senior franchise experience.”

South Africa’s leading rugby schools, with their specialist coaches, sophisticated conditioning programmes and fiercely contested inter-school fixtures, are effectively a network of rugby academies funded by educational institutions.

SA Rugby is increasingly harnessing that expertise. In 2025, four school coaches, all qualified to World Rugby Level 3, were appointed to the national schools and under-18 structures under the mentorship of Junior Springboks head coach Kevin Foote.

At the time of our conversation, 17 schoolboy coaches were due to spend time with Foote’s staff. School coaches also accompany players to Elite Player Development camps, sharing feedback among colleagues back home.

South Africa’s greatest structural advantage, however, might exist on the next rung of the ladder.

Launched in 2008 and co-founded by former Springbok captain Francois Pienaar, the Varsity Cup initially comprised eight universities before the introduction of the second-tier Varsity Shield in 2011. National television coverage afforded student athletes unprecedented exposure while the tournament became a laboratory for experimental laws.

You can’t keep up the facade of being someone else or having somebody else’s personality under pressure.

Among its 61 Springbok graduates are Eben Etzebeth, Handré Pollard, Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche and Kurt-Lee Arendse. Less celebrated is its significance as a finishing school for coaches.

“The Varsity Cup put me on the radar as a coach,” Stormers head coach John Dobson told the competition’s website in 2021.

Franco Smith won the tournament with the University of the Free State in 2015 and was appointed Cheetahs head coach within a month. He subsequently coached Italy before guiding Glasgow Warriors to the 2024 United Rugby Championship title.

Together with community club competitions, the SA Cup and Currie Cup, the tournament allows coaches to hone their craft in progressively more demanding environments before taking charge of professional teams.

But the existence of a ladder does not guarantee that everyone is permitted to climb it.

Jonathan Mokuena, a former Springbok sevens captain who guided North-West University to their maiden Varsity Cup title in 2016, has questioned whether success at university level translates into professional opportunities.

“Your success should also be your selector, but sometimes, unfortunately, that doesn’t happen,” Mokuena told IOL in 2020, identifying provincial unions as particularly important gatekeepers.

In South Africa, the question of who gets those opportunities is inseparable from race.

In 2022, 101 candidates were nominated by provincial unions for SA Rugby’s bespoke Elite Coaching Programme aimed at developing black coaches. Of the 18 selected, only 11, including Mokuena, completed the intensive 18-month programme.

title: Botham back as Morgan-Williams to make first start
article_text:
Wales flanker James Botham has been recalled by head coach Steve Tandy as one of five changes for the Nations Championship finale against Japan at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

In the only backline alteration for the game in Twickenham, Ospreys scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams will make his first Wales start, with Tomos Williams named among the replacements.

Exeter lock Dafydd Jenkins will captain the side for the first time in more than two years with regular skipper Dewi Lake and flanker Jac Morgan also dropping to the bench.

Prop Rhys Carre and hooker Ryan Elias make their first starts of the November campaign, while lock Adam Beard returns at the expense of Ben Carter.

Wales have named an experienced bench that includes 294 caps.

Botham produced a player-of-the-match display in the 35-28 victory against New Zealand after making 30 tackles but was left out of the 29-26 defeat by Australia in favour of Cardiff colleague Alex Mann.

It was a decision which Botham’s father Liam, himself a former Cardiff wing, said Tandy had got wrong.

“I know there's a lot been spoken about it,” said Tandy.

“Everyone has got their opinions and people generally tell you who should be in the team and they never tell you who shouldn't.

“We're a tight group and as a coach I make sure I speak to all the players before if they are not selected. There'll be reasons why, whether it be bigger picture or whether it is form.

“I'll always speak to those, that's a special thing and the connection we feel in our environment.”

Botham, who became a father earlier this week, will play at open-side flanker against Japan after starring at blind-side against the All Blacks, with Mann and number eight Aaron Wainwright completing the back row.

“James was outstanding against the All Blacks, but we've got a back row depth there that we can move things around and freshen things up," said Tandy.

“James has had his little one, he's coming back in full of energy. We were so pleased for him things have gone well there."

Ospreys number nine Morgan-Williams is preparing for his first start in a position that has been dominated by Saracens scrum-half Williams during the Tandy era.

Williams has started 14 out of the 15 internationals, including the previous 11, with opportunities in short supply for others. But Williams came off early in the second half against Australia with a groin problem.

Carre, named Welsh rugby writers player of the 2025-26 season, is given his first start this autumn, with Nicky Smith dropping out of the squad.

Saracens loose-head Carre missed the first month of the season because of a hamstring injury and his only appearance of the autumn Tests so far was off the bench against Japan.

Elias, a replacement in the three previous November internationals, is handed his first Test start since the 2024 Six Nations match against France.

Montpellier lock Beard returns after missing the loss to Australia after suffering a shoulder injury against New Zealand.

Scarlets wing Ellis Mee is given his first involvement in the campaign after being named as a replacement.

Tandy has settled on his backline with full-back Blair Murray, wing Louis Rees-Zammit, centres Eddie James and Max Llewellyn and fly-half Sam Costelow starting all four matches in the November campaign as well as prop Archie Griffin and Jenkins.

Uncapped quartet Che Hope, Macs Page, Rhys Barratt and Aneurin Owen are among the players who will not be given game time, alongside Liam Belcher, Tom Rogers and Seb Davies, while Keiron Assiratti and Jarrod Evans have been late call-ups.

Wales have won three and lost three of their six Nations Championship matches to finish fifth in the northern hemisphere group, a position matched by Japan in the southern hemisphere section.

Wales will face Eddie Jones’ Japan side for a fifth time inside two years with Wales winning three out of the four games.

It is the first match of a Saturday double-header, with England and New Zealand to follow.

“We were frustrated and disappointed with losing last weekend,” said Tandy.

“We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been but there were a lot of positives in the performance to take also.

“We want to go out there, be ruthless and show improvement on our previous performance against Japan."

Jones has picked Auckland-born Tiennan Costley, normally a flanker, on the wing in a side again led by co-captains Warner Dearns and Naoto Saito.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams: Costelow, Morgan-Williams; Carre, Elias, Griffin, D Jenkins (capt), Beard, Mann, Botham, Wainwright.

Replacements: Lake, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, J Morgan, T Williams, Hawkins, Mee.

title: Marco van Staden disciplinary verdict: Five days on from Springboks red card
article_text:
Springboks supporters are still waiting to discover the outcome of Marco van Staden's disciplinary proceedings following his red card against Ireland.

The South African forward was sent off during Saturday's defeat in Dublin, leaving his availability for Sunday's Nations Championship final against France in doubt.

The wait comes at a particularly frustrating time for South Africa, with Pieter-Steph du Toit already ruled out of the final through injury.

Damian Willemse has also been forced to withdraw, leaving the Springboks facing a selection headache ahead of their showdown with France at Allianz Stadium.

Any suspension for Van Staden would further limit South Africa's back-row options.

With the inaugural Nations Championship final just days away, a decision is expected before the weekend.

However, no official timeframe for the announcement has been confirmed.

The disciplinary panel will determine whether the red card should be upheld and whether any further punishment is necessary, in accordance with World Rugby's disciplinary regulations.

RUCK will update this article with the full disciplinary verdict as soon as it is officially announced.

- Nickname: ‘Eskom’, because of his powerful tackling.

- Did you know? Van Staden played scrum-half for much of his schoolboy career before switching to the back row.

- Versatility: He has also played at hooker for the Springboks.

title: Cheslin Kolbe arrives in England ahead of Nations Championship final
article_text:
Cheslin Kolbe has arrived in London ahead of Sunday's Nations Championship final between the Springboks and France. Nothing suspicious about that, surely?

The double World Cup winner has been enjoying the sights of the English capital, sharing pictures from outside Buckingham Palace on Instagram with the caption: “Debut in London for her 🇬🇧”.

A bit of sightseeing, a curry and a romantic getaway. Lovely stuff.

Meanwhile, Damian Willemse and Pieter-Steph du Toit have been ruled out of Sunday's final, with SA Rugby confirming that Erasmus is still considering whether to call up a replacement.

Under any other international coach, this would be a completely innocent city break. Unfortunately for France, Rassie Erasmus has spent years making rugby fans question absolutely everything.

This is the man who turned a seven-one bench split into a genuine tactical weapon and had an entire rugby nation discussing the meaning of coloured traffic lights.

Would anyone really be surprised if Kolbe's sightseeing trip suddenly took an unexpected turn?

Home and Away Rugby even commented on his Instagram post: “See you on Sunday brother 🤝🇿🇦”.

Almost certainly a reference to attending the final as a spectator, but let's not allow common sense to spoil a perfectly good conspiracy theory.

Someone check whether he packed his boots.

There is, of course, no confirmation that Kolbe will join the Springboks squad.

The most likely explanation is that he is enjoying a well-earned break before cheering on his teammates from the stands at Allianz Stadium.

Although, judging by his holiday snaps, there's some serious carbohydrate loading going on. That portion of rice wasn't small.

Imagine trying to explain to your other half that a romantic weekend in London has suddenly turned into 80 minutes against France.

Perhaps Fabien Galthié should keep half an eye on the team sheet.

With any other international coach, I'd dismiss the idea entirely.

title: Six players to watch at the 2026 HSBC SVNS 3 in Dubai
article_text:
To say there the cream of the crop of sevens rugby will be taking the field in Dubai this weekend will be an understatement, with even the HSBC SVNS 3 competition stuffed to the brim with game-busting talent.

The respective qualifiers from regional tournaments in Africa, South America, North America Asia, Oceania and Europe, the 12 teams and 11 nations will feature some serious talent, with several having already played at Rugby World Cups, won major awards and more.

RugbyPass highlights six key players fans should keep an eye out for in the SVNS 3 competition, and who could potentially contribute to their sides qualifying for SVNS 2.

Starting with the Lady Cranes, Peace Lekuru played a major part in Uganda’s defeat of Kenya’s Lionesses 19-14 to qualify for this event in the Africa Rugby Sevens, scoring two key tries.

However, what was even more impressive was how well the Ugandan delivered under pressure, her second try coming in the final play of the game – and should her side push deep into the women’s tournament again, she will likely be called upon to deliver.

In a similar capacity, Zimbabwe find themselves in a similar place, surprising several teams in their Africa Rugby Sevens tournament to qualify for the men’s SVNS 3 – their victory seeing them defeat Uganda 26-19 in Kampala.

Ablant Tavonga had a big tournament for the Cheetahs, but his finest moment came with a try in the dying stages. His side will be hoping he can pull something similar out of the fire, with Zimbabwe facing tough competition in Hong Kong China, Samoa and Canada.

China might have come last in the inaugural season of SVNS 2 earlier this year, but all signs point to a side that is on the rise, having pushed Japan’s Sakura 7s team all the way in the Asia Rugby Sevens and at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.

Yue Sun had a big campaign in both Japan and Sri Lanka, scoring all of her side’s points as they went down 14-7 to Japan in the final in Colombo – but with the result seeing them earn SVNS 3 qualification, the playmaker will look to show what she can really deliver in Dubai.

One of Hong Kong China’s most important dual internationals, Harry Sayers has been kept busy over the last few months, featuring heavily in his side’s World Nations Cup XVs campaign and their gold medal victories at the Asian Games and Asia Rugby Sevens series.

With him set to head to Australia in 2027 for the Rugby World Cup, a big victory for him and his side will come if they can qualify for SVNS 2, finishing in third last year and just missing out.

Samoa is set to be a significant wildcard in both their men’s and women’s sides this weekend, the only country to feature both their teams in SVNS 3 – however, with their women’s team fresh off the 2025 Rugby World Cup, expect them to bring a lot more experience to the forefront.

Their co-captain Saelua Leaula is one such player and is set for a critical campaign, delivering experience in a side that includes three debutants – but a time that oozes talent and potential if they can hit the ground running.

Lastly, the only side defending a SVNS 3 title, Canada’s men’s side will be looking for a better campaign this year after failing to qualify for the SVNS World Championship, finishing last in SVNS 2.

The Maple Leafs will bring in several players with Test rugby experience – several of whom are fresh off the Nations Cup – but the biggest to watch is two-time Major League Rugby title winner Brock Webster, who is the incumbent Major League Rugby Player of the Year after starring for the Chicago Hounds in the grand final.

title: 'I've spoken to all the players': Dave Rennie on the impending All Blacks exodus
article_text:
Rugby World Cups are both a celebration of the international rugby arena and the end of the road for some of its most dedicated warriors. On the latter point, dominoes are starting to fall for New Zealand.

Luke Jacobson has signed with Aviron Bayonnais in the first overseas deal to be announced, and Beauden Barrett is reportedly also Europe-bound with a Bristol Bears deal in place. Plenty more established All Blacks stars are off-contract after 2027, including captain Ardie Savea, who has described the coming Super Rugby season as his ‘last dance’, while Richie Mo’unga and Shannon Frizell only returned to New Zealand from Japan on short-term deals to compete for inclusion at the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Several younger players’ contracts will also expire next year, including Wallace Sititi, who has been linked with Stade Français, while Fehi Fineanganofo will join Newcastle Red Bulls. All players who leave New Zealand forgo their All Blacks eligibility under New Zealand Rugby’s current laws.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie himself is not contracted beyond the coming Rugby World Cup, but says he is across the current contract negotiations and that it would be hypocritical of him to warn his players against leaving New Zealand.

“I’m not surprised because I know about it. I’ve spoken to all the players who are maybe being mentioned,” Rennie told reporters in London.

“I think Luke’s official; any other stuff is unconfirmed, so I probably can’t talk about it yet. But I understand it. When you talk about Luke and other guys who played for 10-plus years in New Zealand, they’ve got an opportunity to make serious money, and it’s also getting exposed to a different culture and different lifestyle and that sort of thing, which is pretty exciting for family.

“So, I understand that you obviously want to keep players at home, but I mean I did the same as a coach. So it would be hypocritical of me to say you shouldn’t go.

“But ultimately, when we’ve got young players who are looking to go, you want to keep them, because you think they can play a hell of a long time in an All Black jersey. But some of those guys will sign for a couple of years, and a couple of years ends up being probably 17 months because they go at the end of an All Black season, and there’s about seven months left of the competition against whether it’s France or Japan or whatever, and then another year. So maybe 19 months they are away prior to coming back.”

Leicester Fainga’anuku is another whose contract runs only until next year, just two seasons after returning from a two-year stint in the Top 14 with Toulon. His decision, like Mo’unga’s and Frizell’s, could become the blueprint for young players within Rugby World Cup cycles.

Rennie isn’t opposed to players developing overseas and returning, given the benefits it’s delivered to the likes of Jordie Barrett and Rieko Ioane during their one-year sabbaticals at Leinster.

“I think it definitely depends on where you go to,” he explained. “I would say the same with guys going to Japan. If the guys can make massive money, then maybe it doesn’t matter where you go. But if your plan is to go away and come back better, then you choose wisely.

“So obviously Leinster’s a high-quality club, always in the race for titles. Yeah, and then I think obviously those guys get into play with a lot of the Irish internationals who are very smart; they’ve got good game sense and game awareness, and so they would have learned heaps.

“Good people involved from a staffing point of view. So there is no doubt that going to a quality club, you come back with an appreciation that the game is played a little bit differently. And so you look at Leinster, very, very structured. There’s no doubt that guys are coming back better.

“And even with a sabbatical, these guys are going away for a year; if they go to really good clubs, potentially they come back, outside of the fact maybe a bit richer, but a bit better, because they’ve been exposed to something different.”

title: ‘Throw the shackles off’: What Les Kiss wants from Wallabies against Ireland
article_text:
It’s been an up-and-down year for the Wallabies, who have claimed some historic wins and fallen to some comprehensive defeats. But as the Aussies now look to their final Test before a Rugby World Cup year, coach Les Kiss wants to see them “throw the shackles off” in attack.

Kiss succeeded Joe Schmidt as the new Wallabies head coach earlier this year, speaking often since then about the ‘Wallaby way’ and the team’s intent on doing the sports-mad nation proud. And in that time, the Wallabies have achieved some special feats.

The Wallabies claimed an unprecedented series victory away to Los Pumas earlier this year, winning the first Test and drawing the second. That match was followed by a memorable win over the Springboks in Perth, before a string of heavy defeats to fierce rivals.

New Zealand (twice) and England both put at least 43 points on the Aussies, who also fell in a closely fought battle with Scotland. But after bouncing back with a hard-earned result against an improving Welsh outfit, the Wallabies have their sights set on a season finale in London.

The Wallabies are preparing to face an Irish side who just beat the Springboks, battling for fifth place in the Nations Championship Finals Weekend. Kiss has identified some areas the Aussies must get right, hoping they can finish the 2026 off on a positive note.

“I hope the performance is one that the boys can really stretch their confidence and belief in the type of game they’re really working to,” Kiss said.

“We need to get the set-piece right, we need to get our defence right. We definitely need to do that. But in attack, hopefully they can throw the shackles off a bit and find a few things stick a bit more for them.

“I’d just like them to finish in a really strong way.

“It’s going to be tough against Ireland for sure. They’re a quality team and what they did to South Africa was tough last week. But go out there and give their all, be a team that makes Australia proud and let’s see what happens. It’ll be a good game.”

Kiss has sprung some selection shocks ahead of the season finale, with regular skipper Harry Wilson and 2026 John Eales Medallist Fraser McReight both shifting to the bench. 95-Test Wallaby Kurtley Beale is also in line to play his first Test in five years.

Former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm and NSW Waratahs scrum-half Teddy Wilson are both set to make their Test debuts. Kalani Thomas also comes into the starting side, with Ryan Lonergan and Tate McDermott both making way.

But the biggest talking point from Wednesday’s team announcement was the selection of Allan Alaalatoa as co-captain, in what will be the tighthead prop’s 100th cap. Alaalatoa joins Isaac Kailea and Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the front row.

“He carries the legacy of the jersey in such a beautiful way. He’s a wonderful character. His leadership style is unbelievable,” Kiss explained.

“The way he can hold a person to account and challenge them is really special. He can do it in a good way, in a tough way, but still be kind at the same time. People listen to him.

“He’s an impressive character. He’s someone that everyone looks up to.”

title: SALT, sisterhood and LA28: Fiji women’s rugby sevens is back on the rise
"Question of balance" - Steve Borthwick explains decision to leave Henry Pollock out
article_text:
Steve Borthwick has explained his decision to leave Henry Pollock on the bench for England's clash with the All Blacks on Saturday.

The Northampton Saints sensation has been one of England's standout performers this autumn, but Exeter Chiefs forward Greg Fisilau has been preferred in the starting XV.

The decision has divided supporters, with many questioning what more Pollock needs to do to earn a starting spot.

However, Borthwick insists the youngster is not the only player pushing for promotion from the bench.

“I enjoy what Henry has done off the bench,” said Borthwick.

“Another one, George Martin, a number of us could say, ‘George Martin has had so much impact, he could start’. It’s not just Henry, there’s a number of people.

“Marcus – every time Marcus comes on, how well does he play? Every time. These guys are doing such a good job at the end of games. They do such a good job in that latter third of the game.”

Remarkably, all eight of Pollock's England tries have come from the bench.

The 21-year-old's effectiveness against tiring opposition appears to be a major factor behind Borthwick's decision.

Borthwick also explained that Fisilau's ability at the breakdown influenced his selection against the All Blacks, who will be without injured superstar Will Jordan.

“There is always the question of balance. The balance of how many changes, the balance of what changes,” Borthwick continued.

“I talked about the breakdown, which is significant, and suits Greg’s skill set. I also like Henry coming on and playing against tired defenders with a bit more space.”

Ironically, Pollock's sensational performances from the bench may be working against his chances of becoming a regular starter.

With England recording a commanding 37-12 victory over New Zealand last weekend, Borthwick clearly sees little reason to abandon a winning formula.

For now, one of English rugby's brightest young talents remains its most dangerous replacement.

title: Two nations remain banned from Rugby World Cups after failed appeal
article_text:
Russia and Belarus remain banned from international rugby, with a bid to overturn Russia's suspension proving unsuccessful.

Both nations have been excluded from international competition since February 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

World Rugby imposed an indefinite suspension on both countries, preventing their national teams from participating in international rugby and cross-border competitions.

Russia's attempts to overturn the suspension have so far failed to secure a return to international rugby.

Neither nation will feature at the expanded 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia, which will see 24 teams compete for the Webb Ellis Cup for the first time.

Russia previously appeared at the 2011 and 2019 Rugby World Cups, facing the likes of Ireland, Australia, Scotland and Japan across those tournaments.

However, Russia has not featured at the tournament since its appearance in Japan.

Belarus, meanwhile, has never qualified for a Rugby World Cup.

Before its suspension, Russia had ambitions to become a more prominent force in international rugby.

The country had even expressed an interest in hosting the 2031 Rugby World Cup, which was subsequently awarded to the United States.

Russia also hosted the Rugby World Cup Sevens in Moscow in 2013.

Those ambitions have since been put on hold.

World Rugby's original suspension was imposed indefinitely rather than for a fixed period.

That means there is no automatic return date for either nation.

With the 2027 tournament now out of reach, the 2031 Rugby World Cup in the United States represents the next potential opportunity.

However, both countries would need to have their suspensions lifted and successfully navigate the qualification process.

For now, their international rugby exile continues.

title: Alaalatoa hits 100 for Wallabies as fellow veteran ends 4-year Test exile
article_text:
Veteran prop Allan Alaalatoa will become the 14th Wallabies centurion when he runs out onto Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, against Ireland on Friday night.

Ten years have passed since Alaalatoa made his debut against New Zealand in a 42-8 defeat at the ANZ Stadium in Sydney.

He will co-captain the side with Harry Wilson, who drops to the bench, for the Wallabies’ final Test of 2026.

After patiently waiting for his first cap, Sydney-born James Ramm has been brought into the team on the wing.

A one-time Olympics gymnast hopeful, Ramm makes his debut in the country where he rediscovered his love for the game during a spell at title-winning Northampton Saints.

Now with Western Force, the 28-year-old is joined in the matchday 23 by another uncapped player in reserve scrum-half, Teddy Wilson.

The former Junior Wallabies captain in line to become the 16th son of a Wallaby to pull on the gold jersey, following in the footsteps of his father David who featured in two Rugby World Cups, including the 1999 side that lifted the Webb Ellis Cup in Cardiff.

A quarter of a century ago, his father played his club rugby across the road from the Allianz Stadium at the Twickenham Stoop after signing for the world-famous Harlequins.

Elsewhere, Kurtley Beale has earned a remarkable recall to the gold jersey – named on the bench, four years since his last Test appearance. Beale is four caps behind Alaalatoa and has made more appearances for the Wallabies than the starting back-three combined.

Kalani Thomas has earned his first Test start at scrum-half alongside club teammate, Carter Gordon.

Wallabies Head Coach Les Kiss said: “Reaching 100 Test matches for your country is a remarkable achievement and it’s only fitting that Allan leads the side out as co-captain for such a monumental occasion.

“He is a talismanic figure within the group, and I know the whole squad and support staff will be doing everything they can to make this rare milestone a memorable one for him, his family and for us.

“We’ve taken some steps forward, grown our game and tested our squad depth this year as a squad and I know the team is highly motivated to put in a performance that reflects the hard work put in by everyone in our final Test.”

title: South America Rugby World Cup 2035 Bid Takes Step Forward
article_text:
As part of the formal bidding process, a multinational working group had already completed a detailed questionnaire covering every proposed venue and host nation. The subsequent online meeting allowed the South American delegation to formally present its vision to twelve Rugby World Cup representatives joining from London and Dublin, followed by a Q&A session addressing specific inquiries.

(A). The Power of Amateur Club Culture: Officials emphasized the central social, familial, emotional, and sporting role of local clubs across the region, positioning grassroots rugby as a foundational pillar of the tournament.

(B). World-Class Tourism: Supported by a promotional video, the delegation highlighted the diverse destinations awaiting visiting fans across the four nations and wider continent—from Patagonia and Iguazu Falls (bordering three countries) to the Atacama Desert and the beaches of Punta del Este and Rio de Janeiro.

(C). Proven Event-Hosting Capacity: The bid underscored South America’s track record of successfully staging massive global gatherings, citing the Olympic Games, the Youth Olympic Games, the FIFA World Cup, major international concerts, MotoGP, Formula One, and Pope Leo XIV’s recent visit to Uruguay and Argentina, which drew millions of attendees with seamless organization.

Former Puma Horacio Agulla, a three-time World Cup veteran (2007, 2011, and 2015) and active member of the bid team, noted that the presentation was warmly received.

“Since it was a Zoom call, we could have done it from an office, but we wanted the importance and symbolism of the clubs as the center of our bid to be crystal clear. It is a differentiator that we are looking to leverage”

“We are convinced that a World Cup in our region will have full stadiums, all the appeal of tourism, and—as an X-factor—the passion and love we feel for rugby, which is born in the clubs.”

The next phase of the candidacy will be an on-site technical visit by Rugby World Cup officials to inspect each proposed venue across the region. Following that tour, additional questionnaires and evaluations will take place in early 2027 to finalize assurances before the World Rugby Executive Board selects and announces the 2035 host in November 2027.

title: Greg Fisilau to make England debut start in blockbuster All Blacks rematch
article_text:
Greg Fisilau will make his first England start against the All Blacks on Saturday with Steve Borthwick making five changes to his side for this weekend’s rematch with New Zealand, recalling Freddie Steward at full-back.

Fisilau, 23, has impressed in England’s three victories to date as a replacement and earns his first start in the No 7 jersey with Ben Curry dropping to the bench. Elsewhere, there are starts for Tommy Freeman on the wing as well Ellis Genge and Luke Cowan-Dickie in the front row.

Borthwick’s decision to start Fisilau means Henry Pollock remains on the replacements bench but it is a richly deserved start for the Exeter back-rower. He was singled out by the head coach for his cameo against Japan and has the opportunity on Saturday to further advance his claim for a place in next year’s World Cup squad.

Steward comes back into the side at full-back with George Furbank dropping out of the 23-man squad. The Leicester No 15 replaced Furbank against Japan because the Harlequins full-back was struggling with a groin problem but Borthwick has given Steward the nod for tactical reasons this weekend.

Up front, Borthwick has opted to start Genge and Cowan-Dickie with Fin Baxter and Jamie George dropping to the bench. Freeman’s recall, meanwhile, was expected after he was a late withdrawal from the 37-12 victory over the All Blacks last weekend with a thigh injury.

The rest of the squad is unchanged with Joe Heyes continuing at tighthead prop and the captain Maro Itoje partnering Alex Coles in the second row. Ollie Chessum continues at blindside flanker while Ben Earl is again at No 8 after his man-of-the-match performance last weekend.

Jack van Poortvliet stays at scrum-half with Fin Smith wearing the No 10 jersey while Seb Atkinson and Henry Slade stay at centre. Will Joseph makes his third consecutive start on the wing. On the bench, Will Stuart joins Baxter and George as front-row cover while George Martin is one of six forwards among the replacements. Archie McParland and Marcus Smith are the backs.

Borthwick’s side are chasing a record third straight victory over the All Blacks as they bid to finish third in the inaugural Nations Championship. “To have the opportunity to play New Zealand again is something the players are really looking forward to,” said Borthwick. “We know the quality New Zealand have and the challenge they’ll bring across the field. For us, it’s about building on last Saturday’s performance, maintaining the standards we set and finding that same level again.”

Meanwhile, South Africa have refused to send a coach to the Nations Championship finals weekend media day at Twickenham with only the captain Siya Kolisi expected to attend. With Rassie Erasmus serving a six-match suspension for his remarkable rant, in which he questioned whether officials were “match-fixing” this month, the Boks are the only one of the 12 competing nations not represented by a coach at the midweek event.

All nations taking part were obliged to send their coach and captain for a series of media appearances. It is understood that the Springboks will not be fined for their coaches boycotting the event before their contest the final against France on Sunday.

This week, the South Africa assistant coach Mzwandile Stick conducted a press conference in his mother tongue of Xhosa to avoid being misinterpreted. When speaking the week before, Stick made comments about the decision by a disciplinary panel to clear Sam Prendergast to play for Ireland against South Africa which could yet land him in hot water.

The fly-half was cited for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji but later cleared. Stick said: “If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle. But it’s an Irish player, it’s free to play.”

Erasmus’s ban came after he claimed officials had missed 17 knee-drop tackles committed against his side in their defeat by France, suggesting that incidents of foul play are not being picked up in what he described as a “manipulation of the game” and that officials are showing more leniency to northern hemisphere teams.

When serving the first match of his ban Erasmus set up an 18+ watchalong in which supporters were able to view the head coach sitting in a Dublin hotel room while he watched their narrow defeat by Ireland. Erasmus has already named South Africa’s side to face France but will be forced into a change with Pieter-Steph du Toit ruled out through injury.

title: Special Goals for USA Teams at Dubai 7s
article_text:
The SVNS season kicks off Saturday with the USA in an unusual position for both teams.

This is the all-important Olympic qualifying season, but for the Eagle men and women, they don't need to worry about it. The USA is the host nation, so the Eagles are in.

This is, of course, very good news for Canada, especially the Canadian men, who are in SVNS 2, because it opens up that North American spot.

As for the Dubai 7s, then, the Eagle teams have some grace to test some things. However it would really be an opportunity for both teams to build on the positives from last year.

The men, of course, somehow pulled out dramatic victory after dramatic victory to get back to SVNS 1, and will want to start strong.

Of course, it won't be easy. The USA is in a pool with Australia, Argentina, and South Africa. They will be sorely tested.

“It’s exciting to be back in SVNS 1," said USA Men's 7s Head Coach Zack Test. "[It] gives us back the regular season and the freedom to look at new players and new combinations, so approaching our first tournament, we want to put out our best squad, but in that best squad, we will run out some new debutants and get them understanding what it takes to play at the SVNS 1 level.

"Over the past two weeks, we’ve been looking at their DNA, and how they like to play and the tactics they like to use. We've been discussing how we want to attack, how we want to defend and trialing this at training so we can anticipate what they're going to bring towards us."

title: Four banned by new World Rugby ruling as Springboks boss Erasmus joined by others
article_text:
World Rugby's clampdown on the abuse of match officials has resulted in another ban.

Romania defence coach Benjamin Lapeyre has been hit with a two-match ban for "disrespecting the authority of match officials" during their Nations Cup defeat to Canada on the weekend. Romania were beaten 27-26 in Bucharest, with Lapeyre having been serving as water carrier during the match.

The former full-back - who turned out for the likes of Toulon and Brive in his playing days - was reported to have been repeatedly challenging the referee's decisions during the match, including making comments about the performance of the TMO.

Challenges were also reportedly aimed towards the assistant referee.

As part of World Rugby's new match official abuse sanction process, an independent panel will now consider such conduct and is able to issue an automatic sanction.

Having reviewed the evidence, Lapeyre's actions were deemed to amount to disrespecting the authority of a match official.

As such, he is banned from all match-day activity, including being present in the stadium, for the duration of the two-match ban.

Lapeyre is the fourth individual to be sanctioned by World Rugby's new process, which was only introduced in the summer.

The most high-profile has been Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus, who was banned for six matches with immediate effect last week.

The South African had made explosive comments in a press conference about refereeing at the start of last week, following his side's narrow defeat to France.

The match official abuse sanction process decided that Erasmus had made comments that suggested "match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials".

On the same day that Erasmus was banned, Hong Kong coach Kane Hames was also hit with a six-match ban for verbal abuse during their Nations Cup match against USA.

Like Lapeyre, Hames was serving as water carrier that day - with offensive language aimed at the officials being picked up on the live broadcast.

Italy head coach Gonzalo Quesada had been the first person banned under World Rugby's new guidelines back in July.

He was automatically sanctioned with a two-match ban after criticising referees in a broadcast interview following their defeat to New Zealand in Wellington.

title: Ireland's Stockdale returns as Beale, 37, back for Wallabies
article_text:
Ulster wing Jacob Stockdale has been recalled to the Ireland line-up for Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off match against Australia.

Stockdale, who was not involved in Ireland's home wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa, replaces Mack Hansen on the left wing.

Nick Timoney comes in for Dan Sheehan at number eight in the only other change to the line-up that started Saturday's 20-17 victory over world champions South Africa at Aviva Stadium.

Sheehan is ruled out of Friday's match at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium (20:10 GMT) after being banned for two games for a croc-roll tackle during the victory over the Springboks.

Tadhg Beirne will captain Ireland in Sheehan's absence for the second time this autumn, having also stepped up against Fiji when Sheehan was ruled out through concussion.

Stockdale returns to the line-up for his 44th cap after a strong start to the season with Ulster, with three tries in as many games.

The 30-year-old started Ireland's Six Nations defeat by France in Paris in February, and while he was not picked against Italy or England, he made a try-scoring return against Wales.

Friday will be Stockdale's first appearance in green since July's Nations Championship victory over Japan.

He is one of eight Ulster players in head coach Andy Farrell's matchday squad. Robert Baloucoune, who starred with two tries against the Springboks, is retained at right wing with Stuart McCloskey kept at inside centre.

With Sheehan out, Timoney returns to number eight. Farrell is dealing with an injury crisis in the back-row position with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen ruled out.

Timoney started at the base of the scrum against Fiji having been preferred to Josh van der Flier at open-side flanker for the Argentina game.

Hooker Tom Stewart and prop Tom O'Toole are retained on the bench alongside Leinster's Thomas Clarkson, who have been dubbed the 'Tom Squad'.

James McNabney is back among the replacements after his eye-catching debut against Fiji was cut short by a concussion.

Nathan Doak, who like Stockdale has not been involved so far this month, is named as the back-up scrum-half.

Despite a taxing win over South Africa, Farrell has opted against making wholesale changes with Andrew Porter, Ronan Kelleher and Tadhg Furlong retained in the front row.

Joe McCarthy and Beirne are kept in the second row with Ryan Baird and Van der Flier alongside Timoney in the back row.

Despite a morale-boosting win over South Africa to round out the Nations Championship campaign with five wins from six games, Ireland finished third in the northern hemisphere standings behind France and England.

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table behind South Africa and New Zealand despite losing four of their six games, including a 33-31 defeat by Ireland in the opening round in Sydney.

Since that game, Joe Schmidt has been replaced as Wallabies boss by former Ireland defence coach and Ulster director of rugby Les Kiss.

Kiss has named two uncapped players in his matchday squad with James Ramm selected on the left wing and Teddy Wilson - son of former World Cup winner David - named as the replacement scrum-half.

The Wallabies bench also features 37-year-old utility back Kurtley Beale, who is set to earn his first cap in five years.

Allan Alaalatoa will co-captain the Wallabies on his 100th cap alongside Harry Wilson, who is named on the bench, while scrum-half Kalani Thomas earns his first Test start after coming off the bench in last weekend's win over Wales in Cardiff.

Ireland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Stockdale; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne (capt), Baird, Van der Flier, Timoney.

Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, McNabney, Doak, Frawley, Aki.

Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Ramm; Gordon, Thomas; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Alaalatoa (co-capt), Canham, Williams, Hooper, Tizzano, Valetini.

Replacements: Nasser, Bell, Tupou, Shaw, Wilson (co-capt), McReight, Wilson, Beale.

title: World Rugby clampdown on match official abuse leads to another ban
article_text:
Romania defence, skills and backs coach Benjamin Lapeyre has been banned for two matches for disrespecting match officials during the Oaks’ 27-26 defeat to Canada in the World Rugby Nations Cup last weekend.

Lapeyre, who was acting as a water carrier at the time, was reported as repeatedly challenging match official decisions during the match, including comments concerning the performance of the TMO and challenges directed at or towards the assistant referee.

An independent panel met and considered the comments and conduct cumulatively and determined that they collectively amounted to disrespecting the authority of a match official.

In line with the provisions of the Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, Lapeyre is banned from all match-day activity, including being present in the stadium, for the duration of the two-match suspension.

Lapeyre is the latest coach to be sanctioned as World Rugby strives to protect the integrity of match officials.

Hong Kong China scrum coach Kane Hames was slapped with a six-match ban for verbally abusing officials during their match with the United States earlier this month, while South Africa boss Rassie Erasmus was sanctioned for the same length of time following controversial comments about match officials after South Africa’s 21-19 defeat to France.

title: World Rugby confirms another ban for disrespecting match officials
article_text:
World Rugby has handed out another two-match suspension as the governing body continues its crackdown on the abuse of match officials.

Romania water carrier Benjamin Lapeyre has been banned following his conduct during the World Rugby Nations Cup clash against Canada in Bucharest on 20 November.

Lapeyre was reported for repeatedly challenging decisions during the match, including comments about the performance of the TMO and challenges directed towards an assistant referee.

An independent panel concluded that his conduct amounted to disrespecting the authority of match officials.

The decision comes amid growing concerns over the treatment of referees, with Hollie Davidson recently receiving widespread support from rugby fans following reports of online abuse.

The suspension means Lapeyre will be banned from all matchday activities for two matches.

He will not even be permitted to enter the stadium during those fixtures.

The punishment falls under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, which was introduced in July 2026.

The new process allows independent panels to punish members of team personnel for inappropriate comments or conduct towards match officials.

Punishments range from guidance letters and formal warnings to suspensions.

World Rugby has previously highlighted how inaccurate comments about refereeing performances from those in positions of authority can fuel online abuse.

The latest suspension serves as another reminder that World Rugby's crackdown extends beyond players and head coaches to all members of the matchday team.

title: Springboks rocked by Pieter-Steph du Toit withdrawal as Rassie delays replacement call
article_text:
Pieter-Steph du Toit has been ruled out of the Springboks’ Nations Championship final against France, Rassie Erasmus has confirmed.

The blindside flanker has withdrawn from the matchday 23 to face Les Bleus, with Erasmus yet to confirm the changes to the team for the meeting at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

Du Toit will return to South Africa along with full-back Damian Willemse, who was omitted from the squad due to an injury he sustained last week against Ireland.

Earlier this week, Ruan Nortje and Ntuthuko Mchunu returned to South Africa, while veteran hooker Bongi Mbonambi linked up with the squad.

Du Toit was named in the run-on team to face France, with his injury now leaving the Springboks with a selection conundrum. Marco van Staden featured against Ireland last week and could come into the 23 but South Africa are still awaiting the verdict of his disciplinary hearing after his red card for a shoulder charge.

“Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus announced on Wednesday morning that flanker Pieter-Steph du Toit has been forced to withdraw from Sunday’s Nations Championship final against France in London due to a niggle and will return to South Africa along with fullback Damian Willemse,” a SA Rugby statement read.

“Erasmus will announce the changes to the match-23 to face Les Bleus later in the week once he has decided whether to call up a replacement player to London.”

Du Toit’s void could be filled by Emmanuel Tshituka, who was named on the bench for the Nations Championship final where he could make his Test debut. The Congo-born loose forward received glowing praise from assistant coach Mzwandile Stick earlier this week.

“We look at Emmanuel and the profile of Pieter-Steph, [who] works hard all day. He’s a world-class player,” Stick said, via Xhosa translator Kuhle “Kooks” Sonkosi.

Ireland international warns Welsh rugby over ditching URC
article_text:
Former Ireland international Alan Quinlan has warned that joining the Gallagher Prem might not change a lot for Welsh rugby.

The Welsh Rugby Union have already approached the Rugby Football Union about getting Welsh sides into the English league. How many sides that would be, as well as if it will actually happen, remains to be seen.

Last week, the Prem announced the first stage of its expansion process - with the league inviting clubs to register their interest in joining the competition.

The Prem hopes to welcome up to two new clubs for the 2029/30 season - although the RFU have remained consistent with their public messaging of prioritising English clubs.

While Welsh clubs are seemingly looking over the border, they do remain committed to the United Rugby Championship for the time being.

And former Munster back-row Quinlan has warned that the grass may not necessarily be greener were they to leave the URC.

“Well, it will obviously have a big impact on the URC if it happens," Quinlan told BetVictor Online Casino. It’s probably something that's been discussed for a while.

“But I just think that the Welsh Rugby Union and Welsh Rugby has been through a lot of turmoil and need to draw breath and be wise.

“There's no guarantee it will work. It could of course so we just don't know.

"But for me, I think the URC is an incredibly competitive league with the South Africans in it.

"I think there's a lot of jeopardy in it right to the end of the season now with playoff positions for Europe.

“I don't see anything wrong with Welsh Rugby.

"I just would wonder and ask the question, ‘What's going to change here by going into the English league with English clubs?’

“For me, I would call for a bit of caution on that one and wait and see.

"I’d say, ‘Be careful for what you wish for.'”

title: Springboks hit by injury blow as Pieter-Steph du Toit ruled out of Nations Championship final

title: World Rugby's England haka fine decision finally revealed
article_text:
England look set to escape punishment for their response to the All Blacks' haka, with common sense seemingly prevailing at World Rugby. Despite the regulations surrounding the traditional Māori challenge and the precedent set at the 2019 Rugby World Cup, no fine has been publicly announced.

Four days have now passed since England's response at Allianz Stadium, which saw players cross the halfway line.

England were famously fined £2,000 at the 2019 Rugby World Cup in Japan after adopting a V-shaped formation in response to the haka.

That decision sparked widespread criticism, with many supporters arguing that teams should be allowed to respectfully respond to the challenge.

The haka is one of rugby's greatest traditions, but the opposition's response can add to the spectacle.

Saturday's scenes generated exactly the sort of excitement and anticipation that international rugby thrives on.

With England and New Zealand preparing to lock horns again this weekend, there appears little appetite for another disciplinary controversy.

World Rugby has yet to publicly confirm its position, but common sense looks set to prevail this time around.
