LIV Golf profane domain names freed up following tour’s demise
article_text:
A tranche of domain names, including livgolfmyass.com, livgolfsucks.com and terroristgolfleague.com, bought up by LIV Golf to prevent critics creating insulting websites could now become available following the company’s liquidation.

The revelation shows how sensitive LIV Golf chiefs were when the controversial league, backed by billions from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, launched in 2022. LIV Golf collapsed after PIF withdrew funding in April.

This column recently revealed that executives were paid millions of pounds before the league filed for bankruptcy, while unsecured creditors, including a UK charity that uses sport to change the lives of vulnerable young people, are not expected to receive a penny back. The Change Foundation, based in Surrey, is owed £22,200.

Executives had hoped a rescue package led by BC Partners would save the league, but the private equity firm walked away due to concerns over the lack of elite players prepared to participate in “LIV 2.0”.

It may be music to the ears of detractors who may – or, indeed, may not – have tried to set up critical websites, only to discover LIV Golf had beaten them to it. Also among the 874 domain names LIV officials bought to keep them out of the hands of naysayers were bloodmoneygolf.com, corruptgolf.com and livgolfracist.com.

LIV Golf did not respond to a request for comment.

The London Stadium has been given the green light to host mega-fights after Newham Council indicated it would grant planning permission to increase its capacity for boxing events.

This column revealed in October that London Stadium bosses wanted restrictions relaxed to allow it to rival Wembley for blockbuster fights and help offset losses from anchor tenant West Ham’s relegation to the Championship.

As part of a wider planning application, officials requested that boxing be classified as a unique one-off event rather than a sport, which limits capacity to 60,000. Newham Council has now resolved to grant permission, subject to final sign-off on the planning agreement.

The stadium has become a £19m-per-year burden on taxpayers since West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in the summer but boxing could help soften the blow.

Anthony Joshua’s upcoming fight against Tyson Fury at the 80,000-seater Principality Stadium is expected to generate more than £20m. Under new terms, a fight night at the London Stadium could accommodate up to 85,000 fans if it is selected in one of eight slots for maximum capacity, while regular events would still be able to sell 80,000 tickets.

The council has requested that London Stadium officials make reasonable efforts to give 100 tickets to local residents.

Newcastle United are still spending money on determining whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new home three years into the project and despite being forced to sell many of their best players in the summer, City AM can reveal.

Sources with knowledge of the situation say both stadium options remain under active consideration. Building a new 65,000-seater ground from scratch at Leazes Park, a Grade II-listed site adjacent to St James’ Park and owned by Newcastle City Council, would be expected to cost around £1.5bn.

Expanding the existing stadium from 52,700 to 60,000 would be a considerably cheaper option at around £500m. The club continues to consult external advisers as it assesses the best course of action.

Newcastle were forced to sell key players in the summer, generating around £240m through the sales of Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, Sandro Tonali to Spurs and Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal.

When Brighton and Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom makes a prediction, he rarely gets it wrong. Now the man who built a fortune by beating the odds through his data-driven betting operation, Starlizard, has predicted that Brighton will qualify for the Champions League.

It would be easy to get carried away with Brighton’s flying start to this season. They have emerged as surprise early challengers at the top of the table, outscoring everyone and beating Arsenal and Manchester City, two of the dominant forces of recent years.

But Bloom is a cool calculator, so a prediction made during an Overcoming Multiple Sclerosis event at the Amex Stadium recently should not be taken lightly.

Aston Villa are considering scrapping their in-house TV channel’s £30 annual subscription fee for season-ticket holders and members after it was pointed out by fans that rival clubs offer a similar service for free.

Currently, season-ticket holders, who pay upwards of £700 per season, receive access to Aston Villa TV at half price. But Villa, who are set to earn at least £50m from playing in this season’s Champions League, will discuss removing the 58p-per-week charge for season-ticket holders and members next year.

title: 'Very Australian': Smith wants Ripper GC name to LIV on
article_text:
Long-time skipper of the all-Australian Ripper GC team, Cameron Smith has outlined his plans for the popular branding following LIV Golf's demise.

Strident junior golf supporter Cameron Smith hopes the Ripper GC name will live on despite the collapse of LIV Golf.

Captain of the all-Australian outfit for four years, Ripper GC drew huge galleries while winning three team events on the Saudi-backed circuit plus the 2024 season-ending championship.

But while the team is no more after LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy, Smith would love to see the Ripper GC brand endure in some shape or form, likely in a junior development capacity.

The 33-year-old former British Open champ established the Cameron Smith Scholarship in 2016 and also contributes to the broader Australian Golf Foundation.

"I would love it too because I think it's a great name and and it's grown a lot of legs the last few years," Smith said ahead of Thursday's first round of the Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.

"It's very Australian and I think a lot of kids have a lot of great memories with it as well.

"But we don't really know where that stands with everything going on, but for sure I would love to do something."

While the likes of LIV peers Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm have polarised during golf's great divide, Smith's reputation as a fan favourite has remained relatively intact.

He proved the Pied Piper of the fairways annually at LIV Golf Adelaide and said he always felt the love of golf galleries around the world and especially at home.

"I've always had great support in Australia," the three-time Australian PGA Championship winner said.

"I'm so thankful for that. (It) was a difficult time for me, so I'm thankful for particularly Adelaide and Australia in general for getting behind me."

His name already etched on the Kirkwood Cup three times, Smith enters this week No.171 in the world after being denied the chance to earn ranking points for years playing in the LIV league.

But after missing six straight cuts at the majors, getting into Sunday contention and finishing seventh at this year's US PGA Championship under new swing coach Claude Harmon had renewed his belief.

"It's been a while since I've been able to perform in a major. I'd just started working with Claude probably two or three weeks before that," Smith said.

"Whenever you make a change, you're really unsure if it was the right decision or not, and that just hit the nail on the head and got the ball rolling and we've been doing the right stuff and the game's felt really good.

"We just need the putts to go in and the results to follow."

title: USGA, R&A provide significant update to golf equipment changes: Answering 5 burning questions
article_text:
The latest twist in the golf ball rollback saga has arrived.

Late last week, the USGA and R&A quietly released a “notice to manufacturers” indicating they have identified two paths to limit distance gains in professional golf and are targeting approval of those changes in time for the start of the new PGA Tour schedule in 2028.

At first glance, the changes outlined by the governing bodies aim to limit distance gains for pro players with the driver and golf ball, but appear to fall short of the distance drops targeted by the golf ball rollback standard initially pursued back in 2023.

But let’s hold on for a second. If you’re a golfer with a normal degree of exposure to governing body minutiae, you’ve probably got no idea what I just said. So let’s get you the goods without the headache in Q&A form.

The USGA and R&A have been looking to curb distance in pro golf for years … but as it turns out, it’s pretty hard to curb distance! Players hate it. Club companies hate it. Regular golfers hate it. The governing bodies don’t even seem to like it.

In fact, it might be said that curbing distance in golf is a lot like eating chard — if it’s so good for you, why does it taste like that?!

The USGA and R&A are unusual in that they are self-aware enough to recognize their chard-iness. They have tried very hard to find a solution to the distance problem that will satisfy everyone or, at least, annoy everyone the least.

First the USGA and R&A pitched a golf ball rollback that would only affect Tour pros. That led to a mutiny. Then, in late 2023, they pitched a rollback for all golfers, pro and recreational. Another mutiny. THEN, in early 2026, they announced a sudden agreement with the PGA Tour to work toward new solutions to curb distance while pushing back the deadline for the rollback-for-all to 2030. No mutiny this time … well, except for all the regular golfers who understood a rollback was necessary to preserve the sport in its purest form. Among that crew? Yep, you guessed it: Mutiny.

Now we have last week’s announcement, which appears to show plans to cut back driver AND golf ball distance … but by what sounds like a smaller margin than the original all-golfer rollback. That’s good news if you didn’t want to lose 15 yards every time you teed off at Bethpage with your buddies. It’s good news if you’re a pro golfer who didn’t want to lose 15 yards at the Masters. And it’s good news if you’re the USGA and R&A and you know you’ve gotta do something to stop the steady creep of distance increases.

2. What is the change the USGA and R&A are promoting?

Basically, they want to make their equipment tests harder to pass. Right now, the equipment companies have wiggle room in how their golf balls and drivers get tested. When the ball is tested, it has a three-yard buffer where it can travel beyond the legal threshold without “failing” the test. When the driver face is tested, it has an 18-microsecond buffer where it can spring beyond the legal threshold without “failing” the test.

Under the changes proposed by the USGA and R&A, which would go into effect in 2028, the driver face and golf ball would be required to stay at or below the legal limit. Considering those changes aren’t aspiring to lessen the distance standard — just test it more stringently — it seems unlikely the changes will produce a considerable distance loss with the golf ball or driver. But a better fence would theoretically defend against continued increases in ball flight.

3. Would *my* golf ball travel shorter if this rule passed?

Nope! These changes are “model local rules,” which means they would be enforced only for the pro tours that choose to adopt them, and not for everyday Joes like you and me.

4. What about that other golf ball rollback? The one you guys have spent three years telling me about?

The rollback for all golfers is still scheduled to go into effect in 2030. That plan, which would change the testing thresholds to lower driving distance for everybody, in theory losing as much as 15 yards off the drives of the longest-hitters, is still ongoing. But it might be on the brink of changing. The 2030 test conditions are being revised, and last week’s notice committed to giving “updated test conditions” to club manufacturers. Earlier this year, GOLF reported that the change could involve the shape of drivers and/or the thickness of the driver face.

At a time of considerable change in professional golf, new distance standards represent the most seismic shift to the game as golfers know it. For years, elite-level players have been gaining distance off the tee — changes driven at least in part by advancements in golf ball and driver technology. These changes, which have changed the way pro golf is played at the highest levels, have concerned the governing bodies responsible for upholding golf’s traditions, its courses and itssense of competitive fairness.

Beyond the historical record and scoring implications of players hitting the ball farther than ever, these changes have threatened many of golf’s most historic tournament hosts. Changes to driving distance have forced many of the world’s best golf courses to undergo costly expansions in order to host high-level men’s events, and have all but eliminated many other historic courses from consideration for such events.

title: Brooks Koepka Aims Yet Another Dig At Bryson DeChambeau
article_text:
Brooks Koepka just can't help himself when it comes to aiming jibes at Bryson DeChambeau, with his latest coming in the build-up to The Skins Game this Friday.

The Farmers Insurance Skins Game will be shown on Prime Video on Friday 27 November with Koepka taking on Justin Thomas, Wyndham Clark and Jackson Koivun at Atlantic Fields Golf Club in Florida.

But although there will be plenty of trash talking between the foursome as they battle it out for $4m - the biggest dig landed in the pre-event press conference was aimed at someone not even taking part.

Koepka was asked about a similar event - The Showdown in 2024 - when he teamed up with DeChambeau in a sign their long-running fued had been squashed.

However, reflecting on that heavy defeat to Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler in the $10m crypto contest Koepka again showed there's no love lost between the two.

"Since I did not win, my teammate didn't hole a putt the entire time, so I did not receive any of that," said Koepka.

"Which is great because it's an individual thing this time. So I'm more excited about that, but it'll be fun."

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

Koepka was also keen to point out he "didn't get to choose" his teammate for that last head-to-head contest.

From fierce enemies to teammates in both the Ryder Cup and then The Showdown, Koepka and DeChambeau were never best buddies but their relationship seemed cordial until recently.

Asked about DeChambeau's experience alongside McIlroy during the final round of the 2025 Masters, Koepka was equally as scathing.

DeChambeau complained about McIlroy blanking him at Augusta National as he finally ended his search for a Green Jacket - with the Northern Irishman wondering why he'd be so chatty when history was on the line.

It was clear which side Koepka was on when he said "I don't think many people want to talk to him regardless" in reference to DeChambeau.

Koepka also said DeChambeau "lives in his own world" during that interview with Skratch's Dan Rapaport and it's clear the two personalties simply don't mix.

DeChambeau is seen more on YouTube than the golf course these days, but if the two ever tee it up in the same event again it'll be one to watch.

Paul Higham is a sports journalist with over 20 years of experience in covering most major sporting events for both Sky Sports and BBC Sport. He is currently freelance and covers the golf majors on the BBC Sport website. Highlights over the years include covering that epic Monday finish in the Ryder Cup at Celtic Manor and watching Rory McIlroy produce one of the most dominant Major wins at the 2011 US Open at Congressional. He also writes betting previews and still feels strangely proud of backing Danny Willett when he won the Masters in 2016 - Willett also praised his putting stroke during a media event before the Open at Hoylake. Favourite interviews he's conducted have been with McIlroy, Paul McGinley, Thomas Bjorn, Rickie Fowler and the enigma that is Victor Dubuisson. A big fan of watching any golf from any tour, sadly he spends more time writing about golf than playing these days with two young children, and as a big fair weather golfer claims playing in shorts is worth at least five shots. Being from Liverpool he loves the likes of Hoylake, Birkdale and the stretch of tracks along England's Golf Coast, but would say his favourite courses played are Kingsbarns and Portrush.

title: Marco Penge puts difficult year behind him to secure PGA tour card
article_text:
Marco Penge pulled off one of the most dramatic escapes in recent golf history at the 2026 RSM Classic. Entering the final week of the season ranked 120th in the FedEx Cup standings, the 28-year-old Englishman needed a top-four finish just to keep his PGA Tour card.

He delivered far more, birdieing the 72nd hole to force a four-man playoff before draining a clutch birdie putt on the first extra hole to claim his maiden PGA Tour title and a two-year exemption. Here is the story behind the resilient golfer who appears to thrive when his back is against the wall.

1. An accidental start at the driving range

Born in Crawley, England, in May 1998, Penge discovered golf purely by chance at age five. His mother bought his father, Angelo, a cheap set of clubs for his 40th birthday to help him relax. Angelo took young Marco along to the Pease Pottage driving range, where the boy picked up a club and immediately striped the ball straight down the fairway.

That natural talent led to formal lessons at Mannings Heath Golf Club and eventually a standout amateur career that was highlighted by winning the 2015 Scottish Amateur Stroke Play Championship.

After turning professional in 2017, Penge took the long road to the top. He honed his craft on the third-tier PGA EuroPro Tour, earning his first pro victory at the 2019 Irish Masters.

He then graduated to the Challenge Tour, where his breakthrough arrived in 2023. That season, Penge won twice, including the season-ending Rolex Challenge Tour Grand Final, to top the Order of Merit and secure his promotion to the DP World Tour.

Penge has been refreshingly open about living with ADHD, explaining that the condition can easily cause him to overthink on the course. Rather than viewing it as a limitation, he has worked closely with his team to build strict routines and mental structures that prevent overstimulation.

Penge credits understanding his own mind as a massive factor in his professional success, noting that the golf course is actually where he feels most at ease.

Penge’s career hit a major roadblock in December 2024 when the DP World Tour handed him a three-month suspension and a £2,000 fine for breaching its integrity program.

An investigation revealed he had placed small bets on golf tournaments between 2022 and 2024. Although he never wagered on himself or events he was competing in, the ban sidelined him heading into 2025. Penge owned up to the mistake, attributing it to a misunderstanding of the rules.

Returning from suspension in February 2025, Penge played with a chip on his shoulder and enjoyed a career-defining year. He captured his maiden DP World Tour title at the Hainan Classic in April, followed by victories at the Danish Golf Championship and the Spanish Open.

He finished second in the Race to Dubai rankings, climbed inside the world’s top 30, reportedly turned down a massive LIV Golf offer, and earned his 2026 PGA Tour card.

Penge’s 2026 transition to the United States tested his resilience to the limit. Following a move to Florida with his wife, Sophie, the couple endured a terrifying stretch when their newborn son spent four weeks in neonatal intensive care.

Simultaneously, Penge battled a debilitating viral illness and vertigo that forced him to step away from golf for six weeks after the PGA Championship.

Slumping in the standings, he arrived at Sea Island needing a miracle – but he delivered in style to turn a season of personal and physical adversity into a career-defining triumph.

title: David Puig’s Ryder Cup Dream Hits A New Road After LIV Collapse
article_text:
David Puig has made his target crystal clear. The 24-year-old Spaniard wants a spot on Europe's 2027 Ryder Cup team. He told reporters that making the squad is "another dream of mine since I was young." This isn't just a side note for the young star. Puig sees the team at Adare Manor next September as his main goal now that the LIV Golf landscape has shifted.

Puig is starting his full season on the DP World Tour this week. He defends his Australian PGA Championship title in Sydney. The field includes major winners like Cameron Smith and Adam Scott. Puig knows the path is steep. In 2026, his world ranking peaked at 56th. A top-20 result was also achieved at the US PGA Championship. But the road to the Ryder Cup requires consistency. "Playing in a Ryder Cup would be amazing," Puig added, according to Golfmagic. "I'll try my best. Hopefully it's enough to be on the team in September."

While Puig chases a player spot, others have already lost their shot at leadership. Ian Poulter confessed he would give up his Ryder Cup captaincy hopes for Europe. He discussed the price he paid after joining the Saudi-backed league. Poulter said he accepted the possibility of losing the role. "Yes, I've sacrificed being a Ryder Cup captain," he said. He understood the rules when he made his move.

The financial hit was real too. The DP World Tour reportedly fined Poulter approximately $1.1 million. The tour confirmed in June 2026 that Poulter settled the debt. That payment did not restore his eligibility for future leadership. The rules state that players who resign their membership cannot become captains. Poulter even compared his earnings to a potential $10 million a year deal with Sky Sports. He described his career earnings as "an obscene amount of money." The message is simple. You cannot play both sides and expect a leadership role.

Puig's situation offers a stark contrast to the LIV fallout. The 24-year-old has not resigned his membership. During the tour's three-week Opening Swing, Puig intends to compete two times. He will skip the Australian Open to play the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa. He wants to see more of the world while building his case for Europe. "It's hard when two great tournaments combine with each other," Puig explained. "It was definitely a tough decision, but I'm looking forward to playing here this week and there next week." His focus remains on the game. "But it starts in weeks like this where playing good golf definitely matters."

European captain Luke Donald is seeking a historic third consecutive victory. The team will face the United States at Adare Manor.

title: Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young and Wyndham Clark headline PGA Tour Player of the Year award nominees
article_text:
The PGA Tour on Tuesday announced nominees for the two major awards it hands out each year, Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year. Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young, Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick and Chris Gotterup make up the five-man race for the Jack Nicklaus Award, while Alex Fitzpatrick, Ben James, Kristoffer Reitan, Jackson Koivun and Marco Penge are among those vying for the Arnold Palmer Award.

Scheffler has become familiar with getting his hands on the Jack Nicklaus Award in recent years. The world No. 1 joined Tiger Woods as the only golfer to claim the title three years in a row when he secured the honor in 2024. After winning it again in 2025, Scheffler can join Woods again as the only players to ever win it five times in a row. The 15-time major champion won the award five straight seasons from 1999-2003 and three straight from 2005-07.

In 2024, Scheffler became the third golfer to be named Player of the Year three times in his career, joining Woods (11 times) and Rory McIlroy (three). He surpassed McIlroy -- who is not nominated for the award for the first time since the 2020-21 season -- by winning the award again last season.

Scheffler's campaign for a fifth straight Nicklaus award appeared in doubt as he went through the PGA Tour regular season with just one victory. He made up for lost time in the postseason by winning the St. Jude Championship and the Tour Championship for his second career FedEx Cup crown.

The 30-year-old finished inside the top 10 in three of the four major championships, had the lowest scoring average on the PGA Tour and missed only one cut this season.

Scheffler's season was one highlighted by consistency, while Clark's was one of memorable achievements. Clark fired a final-round 60 at The CJ Cup Byron Nelson for the first win of his year before grabbing his second career U.S. Open victory at Shinnecock Hills, with Scheffler by his side on that fateful Sunday.

The wins by Scheffler in the FedEx Cup Playoffs sandwiched a win by Clark at the BMW Championship as he got the better of McIlroy in St. Louis.

Clark and Scheffler's win total of three were matched by both Fitzpatrick and Gotterup. Fitzpatrick won the Valspar Championship before edging out Scheffler in a playoff at the RBC Heritage the week after the Masters. The Englishman was not done, however, and scored the biggest win of his season at the Zurich Classic where he helped secure a PGA Tour card for his little brother Alex.

Meanwhile, Gotterup got off to the hottest start with wins at the Sony Open and the WM Phoenix Open. The big-hitting right hander added another at the John Deere Classic to polish off a transformational season.

Gotterup paired up nicely with Young at the Presidents Cup, one year after Young notched his first win on the PGA Tour. He added to his tally in 2026 with wins at The Players Championship and the Cadillac Championship amid a stretch in the spring where he was the hottest player in the world.

The Rookie of the Year race will be just as compelling given the influx of young talent on the PGA Tour in 2026. Five players are in the running with four of them notching victories, including Penge who claimed the season-finale at the RSM Classic to maintain his playing privileges on the PGA Tour in a season where he dealt with injury.

His fellow Englishman, Fitzpatrick, won the Zurich Classic with his brother, Matt, and went onto collect six top-10 finishes in a limited run on the PGA Tour. One of those finishes came at the Truist Championship where Fitzpatrick fell just short to Reitan, who captured the biggest win of any rookie on the PGA Tour in 2026.

Reitan won the signature event at Quail Hollow Club and also had a top-10 finish at The Memorial Tournament. While the Europeans fared well early in the season, the Americans brought the excitement late with Koivun winning the 3M Open in his third start as a professional. The highly touted amateur got the better of Scheffler at TPC Twin Cities to earn the trophy.

Koivun did not have enough rounds to qualify for a scoring average on the PGA Tour in 2026 where James ranks second only to Scheffler. The No. 1 from PGA Tour University started his career at the Canadian Open and has not looked back as all five of his top-10 finishes also doubled as top-five efforts, including his playoff loss at the World Wide Technology Championship.

The honors will be awarded through a voting process, including PGA Tour members who played in at least 15 official FedEx Cup events during the 2026 season. Voting closes on Friday, Dec. 4 with winners announced at a later date.

title: MLB launches preventative suit against MLBPA as lockout looms
article_text:
The elite Major League Baseball (MLB) has filed a class action lawsuit against the MLB Players Association (MLBPA), a preventative move it says is aimed at preventing an antitrust suit being leveled against it by the labor union.

Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) negotiations have shown no sign of bearing fruit, making the prospect of a lockout in 2027, and thus no baseball, likely.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

Now, MLB claims that it has “a reasonable and imminent fear” that the MLBPA intends to use antitrust litigation as a tactic against the league.

MLB is the only major US league with a unique antitrust exemption, granted by the US Supreme Court in 1922, that shields it from federal commerce rules by legislating MLB games as local commerce rather than interstate commerce.

There is, however, a flaw, introduced in 1998 by the Curt Flood Act, which would allow MLB players to sue the league on antitrust grounds individually should the MLBPA be disbanded, as the 1922 exemption does not cover major league players.

The league believes the MLBPA could bring litigation against the league as an alternative to continued negotiations as a means of forcing through what it wants, which is a CBA without a salary cap.

It would do this by decertifying itself, something the league claims would be a ‘sham’ thus allowing the players to sue, claiming a lockout is illegal, and thus exposing MLB to heavy antitrust damages.

In a release, the league said that the suit is a measure “simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season.”

In a rival statement, the MLBPA called the lawsuit ‘frivolous’, saying: “We will respond appropriately, but MLB’s decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.”

With this suit, MLB is seeking to establish firstly that a lockout is fully legal due to its exemption from antitrust law, secondly that even if it is not exempt, it would remain legal as it is now “an unreasonable restraint on trade,” and thirdly that federal courts do not have the jurisdiction to affect the lockout.

MLB is the only one of the four US major sports leagues to not enforce a salary cap, nor does it enforce a spending floor, which in recent years means that a large gap has developed between high-spending teams like the champion LA Dodgers (which has a payroll of around $420 million), and the low spenders like the Miami Marlins (payroll c.$78 million).

Effectively, MLB’s proposal outlines that owners will find it hard to achieve strong market value outcomes for selling their teams without a cap, as new investors would be loathe to spend lavish seven- or eight-figure sums on teams without parity guarantees.

The league claims that without a salary cap, it may find it hard to maintain a competitive balance among franchises, a factor that is harming franchise values, particularly at smaller-market teams.

That claim has taken a hit this season, as the World Series was won by the Milwaukee Brewers franchise, one of the smallest payroll teams in MLB, which swept past the Dodgers in the process.

Indeed, the MLBPA has often rejected narratives surrounding the salary cap as a positive measure, arguing that any cap would only serve to enrich owners, many of whom may not have to spend as much as before to compete, at the expense of players.

In its latest statement, the MLBPA said that MLB owners “continue to propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values.

The fact, then, that the World Series featured two small markets makes it perhaps the most timely edition in years, and one for which the aftershocks will reverberate for a while, despite the fairly elementary conclusion: a 4-1 Brewers win.

In the latest edition of the Sportcal Industry Insights podcast, GlobalData Sport lead analyst Conrad Wiacek and senior data researcher Will Padmore comb through those aftershocks, using data to benchmark the viewership statistics and dissect the league’s sponsorship and media rights strategy, as well as discussing what will come next in the CBA standoff.

This data is included in the GlobalData Sport Post Event Analysis – MLB World Series 2026, available on the GlobalData Sport Intelligence Center, which highlights the major themes surrounding the 2026 World Series, from the commercial partners to the strong attendance numbers (at record prices), and the media value presented by broadcaster Fox.

title: Visma dials back Visma | Lease a Bike sponsorship, remains founding partner
article_text:
Team Visma | Lease a Bike (VLAB), the leading road cycling organization, has confirmed that lead sponsor Visma will no longer serve as the team’s title partner going forward, although it will not completely divest from the team.

Visma has extended its partnership and will remain as a ‘founding partner’ of the team, but has opted not to continue with naming rights, an outcome that has been rumored for months.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

The Norwegian tech brand has been a title sponsor of the team since 2019, and took over the lead sponsorship in 2024.

Visma is now the second such founding partner on the team’s roster after previous lead sponsor Jumbo, the supermarket chain, which stepped back from its role like Visma at the end of 2023.

Now Visma will dial back its commitment, although it will remain the team's official technology partner, and several Visma-owned tech brands will now appear on the VLAB jersey through the 2027 campaign.

Speaking on the announcement, VLAB chief executive Richard Plugge said: “It’s fantastic that Visma is extending its partnership with our team. Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019.

“I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years. Having Visma stay with the team as a founding partner reflects what we’ve built together.”

The departure of Visma leaves a big sponsorship gap that needs to be filled, should the team wish to mount a strong 2027 campaign and avoid losing ground to rivals like Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Lidl-Trek, and Decathlon AG2R La Mondiale, which have all bolstered their portfolios in recent years.

Sponsorship such as this is vital for cycling teams at all levels of the sport, the majority of which are almost entirely sponsor-funded.

If VLAB wishes to remain competitive against major rival UAE Team Emirates – XRG, and, crucially, retain top star Jonas Vingegaard in the long term, then further backing is needed.

The 2026 season was a mixed year for VLAB, with Vingegaard securing the Giro d’Italia Grand Tour general classification easily, but failing to challenge rival Tadej Pogačar in the Tour de France, before dropping out of that race due to injury and ending his season early.

Vingegaard’s position as arguably one of the top-2 riders in the sport will certainly be a key driver of VLAB’s sponsorship sales process. Earlier this week, the team expanded its partnership with major US sportswear brand Nike.

The Dane claimed back-to-back Tour de France wins in 2022 and 2023, as well as a Vuelta a España win in 2025, and the aforementioned Giro win this year, making him only the eighth rider in history to win all three Grand Tours.

Belgian icon Wout van Aert, young Brit Matthew Brennan, and 2023 Vuelta champion Sepp Kuss will also likely have factored into Nike’s plans, as continued broadcast presence at key points in races like the Tour de France is an important driver of sponsorship in cycling.

Before the 2026 Tour de France, VLAB chief business officer Jasper Saeijs suggested that cycling sponsorship fees represent a strong value proposition relative to the media exposure that WorldTour races, particularly the three Grand Tours, bring, saying: “We (VLAB) are one of the best sponsorship opportunities in sports.”

By comparison, Jonathan Vaughters, manager of the EF Education–EasyPost team, argued perhaps the opposite.

Remarking on the state of the sport and the effects of this period of dominance by a few privileged teams, Vaughters said: “The top teams are no longer a valuable proposition from a sponsor standpoint. A company could get its logo on a ninth-ranked Formula 1 [motor racing] team’s car for €20 million ($23.1 million), or they could invest it in a cycling team.

“But €20 million isn’t going to win them the Tour de France. There’s zero chance. Cycling used to be a valuable proposition, but we’ve lost that now.”

Cycling’s heavy reliance on sponsorship revenue, and that spending’s direct correlation with rider contract spending, has created a catch-22 situation where winning races requires top riders, access to top riders requires significant sponsorship revenue, and sponsorship revenue can only be grown by winning races.

This has effectively stratified the WorldTour peloton, with the top six-to-eight teams, backed by high-profile sponsors, billionaire investment, or sovereign wealth financing, performing at a level that the other sides, which rely on less lucrative sponsorship deals and, in many cases, face an annual struggle just to continue operations, cannot.

This dynamic was dissected earlier this year on the Sportcal Podcast, where GlobalData Sport lead analyst Conrad Wiacek and head of data Gordon Berry discussed VLAB's predicament and the varying perspectives on cycling sponsorship, where money in cycling comes from, and how teams can improve sponsorship values by maximizing their resources.

title: Generali expands World Tennis partnership to grassroots programs
article_text:
The World Tennis governing body has extended and expanded its partnership with Generali Group just months after the international insurance company became the title sponsor of the major Davis Cup tournament.

This new grassroots-focused agreement will see the pair collaborate on a number of programs focused on increasing tennis uptake globally among target demographics.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

In all, five programs will be supported throughout the agreement: the Generali World Tennis Masters Tour (a seniors series for players over the age of 30), the Generali Junior Tennis Initiative (a grassroots tennis education program), Generali Coaches For Life (coaching education program), Generali World Tennis Activation (local mass participation events centered around Davis Cup matchups), and Generali Rally Together Fund (money ringfenced for new tennis infrastructure globally).

This deal, with multi-year agreement, includes “significant investment” and has an aim of bringing as many a 1 million new young people into tennis.

World Tennis was rebranded from the former ITTF moniker back in June, a move it said came with plans to raise investment and secure “new and stronger revenue streams” forming part of the governing body’s new strategic vision for the long-term sustainable growth of the sport.

Generali already has a strong presence in tennis, including title sponsorship of the Generali Open in Kitzbühel and a partnership with ATP player Dominic Thiem in Austria, sponsorship of the Monte Carlo Masters event, and partnerships with the Spanish and German tennis federations, alongside the aforementioned Davis Cup deal.

title: LFP secures key court ruling to deploy real-time piracy blocking
article_text:
The LFP, domestic French soccer’s organizing body, has secured a court ruling allowing it to block pirate services during broadcasts of top-flight Ligue 1 and second-tier Ligue 2 matches automatically and in real-time.

The ruling allows internet service providers to block illegal streams under new anti-piracy legislation introduced in August.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

The Paris Judicial Court issued its ruling on November 20, becoming the first to authorise the new blocking mechanism established by France’s law of August 3, 2026, on the organisation and financing of professional sport.

This decision paves the way for the deployment of an automated system that will allow the LFP to identify and block pirate streaming services as they emerge during live Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 matches.

With this development, the LFP will no longer have to rely on the existing process of weekly updates and manual approval by French audiovisual regulator Arcom.

An automated system is expected to become operational in the coming weeks, enabling internet service providers to implement blocking orders without delay, under Arcom’s supervision.

Court rulings obtained by the league last July already allowed for the protection of LFP competitions against pirate services throughout the 2026-2027 season.

In a statement, the LFP said: “This judgment, issued within the framework of the proceedings initiated by the LFP Group against internet service providers to obtain the right to block pirate services in real time, marks a new step.

“For the first time, the LFP Group will be able to rely on the mechanism established by the law of August 3, 2026, to act at the very moment new pirate services appear during the broadcast of matches.

“The automated system necessary for its implementation is expected to be deployed in the coming weeks, under the control of Arcom, in order to allow Internet service providers to implement the ordered blocks without delay.”

Through the new system, the French league body is seeking to “minimize the time between identifying a pirate service and blocking it, in order to prevent access at the very moment when the damage is greatest, during the broadcast of matches.”

The LFP believes the new mechanism will allow it to “significantly increase the speed and effectiveness of its action against piracy and strengthen the protection of its competitions, its broadcasters, and the revenues of professional football.”

The organization added: “The fight against piracy is a major challenge for the professional football economy.

“Protecting content at the very moment it is broadcast means protecting the value of audiovisual rights, the investments made by broadcasters, and the revenue that allows clubs to grow. With this new system, the LFP Group is strengthening its ability to defend one of its most strategic assets.”

The move could boost the LFP’s attempt to secure new domestic broadcast partners after recently launching a tender process.

The tender covers five seasons from the 2027-28 through 2031-32 cycle and represents a U-turn by the body after it originally planned to keep the current broadcast arrangement through 2028-29.

The process went live on November 3 and will run until 3 December, after which bids will be examined the LFP and its LFP Media arm.

The tender contains a single package for all Ligue 1 games each season – as is now permitted under French competition law – as well as the exclusive distribution of Ligue 1+, the league’s OTT streaming platform.

Should a traditional linear broadcaster or streaming service secure the main package of rights, it could spell the end of the road for Ligue 1+, which was launched – mostly out of necessity – in mid-2025, and covered all games from the 18-team Ligue 1 last season.

Ligue 1+ exclusively held the rights to eight of the league’s nine weekly games last season and aired the ninth game (a BeIN exclusive live fixture) on a delay.

The establishment of the in-house platform followed the premature termination of a previous domestic rights agreement between the LFP and global subscription service DAZN.

Ligue 1's domestic media rights have been a source of turmoil and significant concern for the LFP for the last seven years, during which time they have decreased in value significantly.

title: Bodø/Glimt lead global football clubs with 555 per cent social media growth in 2026
article_text:
Bodø/Glimt recorded the highest percentage increase in social media followers among the world’s leading football clubs in 2026, with their combined Instagram and TikTok audience increasing by 555 per cent between 1st January and 17th November, according to data platform Football Benchmark.

The club’s following grew from approximately 136,000 to 888,000, placing them at the top of Football Benchmark’s ranking of the ten fastest-growing clubs by percentage. Their 555 per cent growth rate was more than 2.7 times that of Chicago Fire FC, the second-ranked club, which recorded an increase of 205 per cent, with Turkish side Trabzonspor registering 140 per cent growth closing in the first three clubs with the biggest digital increase. Also worth highlighting is the contrast with Como 1907, the emerging force in Italian football, which ranked fourth with 138 per cent growth – more than five times lower than Bodø/Glimt’s figure. The analysis took into account only clubs with at least 100k total followers across Instagram and TikTok.

Having competed in Norway’s second division as recently as 2017, Bodø/Glimt have transformed their sporting standing through sustained development and consistent performances on the European stage. Last season’s Uefa Champions League campaign, featuring victories over Manchester City and Atlético de Madrid before eliminating Inter, further elevated the club’s international profile.

The figures demonstrate how sporting performance and European competition exposure can accelerate international audience growth, creating opportunities to strengthen brand positioning, expand commercial reach and attract new partners.

Bodø/Glimt’s achievement also highlights the changing dynamics of football’s global attention economy, where ambitious clubs can build significant international audiences through sporting credibility and a distinctive competitive identity, challenging the traditional dominance of established football brands.

Source: Football Benchmark Social Media Analytics Platform. Combined Instagram and TikTok followers, 1 January–17 November 2026.

Empower Sports is a global PR Agency that builds and boosts the brand of clubs, executives, coaches and athletes.

title: Shorts: The Romans, Hull FC, Grand Départ GB
article_text:
The appointment comes as the NBA prepares for NBA Europe, its new league with FIBA, which the NBA and FIBA say will begin play “next fall”. Current target countries include Britain (with London and Manchester as potential host cities), Italy (Rome and Milan) and Germany (Munich and Berlin)

This week the league unveiled a plan targeting at least 10 billion euros (nearly $11 billion) for developing and renovating arenas across Europe. Backers include Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners, J.P. Morgan, Sixth Street and Stonepeak.

The Romans is an independent creative communications agency. Last month it launched a dedicated sports and entertainment practice in the Middle East and North Africa, appointing Sam Buckett as managing director. He joins from Burson in Saudi Arabia, where he led sports and entertainment. The new unit is the agency’s second dedicated sports and entertainment practice after the UK.

Hull FC have signed sports performance brand Nutrition X as their nutrition partner, with players already using its products during the first weeks of pre-season training.

Founded in 2011, Nutrition X supplies performance and recovery products to professional sports clubs and athletes across the UK and Europe. Its sports nutrition range is built around education, science and safety. The brand will work closely with the Black & Whites’ performance and nutrition teams to support players through the 2027 season.

George Gladding, Club Partnership Executive at Nutrition X, said, “We are delighted to be building a partnership with Hull FC, bringing together two organisations that share a commitment to performance, development and success. We’re looking forward to working closely with the club’s performance and nutrition teams, providing the support, expertise and products to help players perform at their best.“

“We see this as the beginning of a long-term relationship and are excited to grow together, supporting Hull FC both on and off the pitch for many seasons to come.”

Grand Départ GB 2027 has appointed LS Events as delivery partner for the first team time trial in the history of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift. The stage will close next summer’s British Grand Départ in London on Sunday 1 August 2027.

Seven-rider teams will race an 18km circuit through central London, starting on Whitehall and finishing on The Mall, where men’s Tour de France stages have finished twice before. Between 21 and 22 teams will compete, setting off at four-minute intervals.

LS Events will bring its experience of pan-London operations to a stage expected to draw hundreds of thousands of spectators along a route passing the Houses of Parliament, the London Eye and Tower Bridge. Across its three days, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift is expected to be the most attended women’s sporting event ever staged in Britain.

Paul Bush OBE, Managing Director, Grand Départ GB, said: “The London stage of next year’s Grands Départs is going to be the finale to an amazing month of world-class sport in communities across Scotland, England and Wales, and LS Events’ experience of delivering major events in London make them the logical choice for Grand Départ GB to partner with. London is already a cycling city, so what better platform to showcase the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift with this amazing team time trial stage that will inspire the next generation of women cyclists.”

Jen-e Jones, Vice President of Operations, LS Events, said: “We’re delighted to be working with Grand Départ GB and the GLA to lead delivery of the stage three London team time trial. It’s one of the most complex sport operations we’ve delivered in the capital, and we’re proud to be the trusted partner for such a landmark event. On one day, the world’s best women riders will race past some of London’s most recognisable landmarks. It’s a pivotal moment for women’s cycling.“

Jones continues to add, “We’re responsible for the extensive logistics and preparation required for the route and operational leadership across the boroughs. That means traffic and crowd management, safety, spectator welfare, working with businesses and communities to ensure everyone benefits from the event, and dressing the city, all powered by Grand Départ JOY Maker volunteers, stewards and the LS Events core team. This will mark the very first Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift event in our capital city, and LS Events could not be prouder to bring our extensive ‘London’ experience to this ground-breaking event.”

In 2027 Britain will become the first nation outside France to host both the men’s and women’s race starts in the same year. The men’s race begins in Edinburgh on Friday 2 July 2027, and the women’s race starts in Leeds on Friday 30 July 2027, with stages from Leeds to Manchester and Manchester to Sheffield before the London finale. The events are supported by funding partners the UK Government, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, UK Sport and British Cycling.

The London stage is estimated to generate £12 million in economic impact for the capital, and marks the Tour de France’s return to London for the first time in 12 years. Organisers are targeting more than 10 million spectators across the six stages, with around 9,000 volunteer JOY Makers involved.

Founded in 2004 and led by Co-CEOs Steve Reynolds and Dave Grindle, LS Events has a portfolio that includes UEFA Champions League Final fan activations, Formula E, Emirates Great Britain SailGP, Soccer Aid, Operation London Bridge, Pride in London and American Express presents BST Hyde Park.

title: Leicester City FC bring in BettaBet as betting partner
article_text:
Leicester City FC have signed UK-based betting platform BettaBet as their exclusive UK betting partner until the end of the 2026/27 season.

Foxes supporters will get access to favourable odds, club merchandise and exclusive experiences through the deal. BettaBet will also appear across Leicester’s digital platforms and on Filbert Way on matchdays at King Power Stadium.

Russell Jones, Leicester City Commercial Director, said: “We’re pleased to welcome BettaBet to our partner network and look forward to building a successful relationship with them. The partnership will provide a platform for BettaBet to connect with our supporters through our digital channels and matchday activity at King Power Stadium.”

Daniel Shannon, VP of Marketing at Betable Group, said: “We’re incredibly excited to be partnering with Leicester City, a club with fantastic history, a passionate fanbase and strong reputation both in the UK and internationally. For us at Betable, this partnership represents another important step in our growth as we continue to strengthen our presence in the UK market.

“We’re looking forward to working closely with the club, bringing fresh ideas to the partnership and building a successful relationship.”

The agreement comes during Leicester’s first season in the third tier since 2008/09. The Foxes were relegated from the Championship in April, a decade after their 2016 Premier League title.

Betable provides the technology behind a number of sportsbooks licensed by the UK Gambling Commission. In the first half of 2026 it brought three brands to the UK market: Ivy Bet, RightBet and Bet442.

title: Twickenham set to be half empty for Nations Championship finals opening night
article_text:
The start of the Nations Championship finals weekend will play out in front of thousands of empty seats on Friday with Twickenham's Allianz Stadium set to be filled to about half its 82,000-seater capacity.

The uppermost tier of the stadium is entirely closed, while just over half of the middle tier is open.

Tickets are on sale closer to the action, with a large proportion of seats in some lower-tier sections, notably in the north-west corner of the stadium, remaining.

The finals weekend is the climax of a new format, which repackages July and November Test fixtures and culminates in six play-off fixtures between northern and southern hemisphere sides over three days.

Friday's double-header fixture begins with Italy and Fiji, the two lowest-ranked nations, playing at 16:40 GMT, before Ireland and Australia meet in the fifth/sixth place play-off at 20:10 GMT.

Sales for Saturday and Sunday's action, which are headlined by England v New Zealand and a South Africa v France grand final respectively, are stronger.

Around 65,000 tickets have so far been bought for each, with momentum fuelled by England's five-game winning streak and France's dramatic win over the Springboks in Paris a fortnight ago.

With the identity of the teams contesting each play-off game only confirmed last weekend however, organisers have been up against time to market fixtures to the public.

Diary and budget constraints in the run-up to Christmas and the fact Allianz Stadium has already hosted capacity crowds for England's victories over Australia, Japan and New Zealand over the previous three weekends have added to the challenge.

A limited amount of 'follow my team' tickets, which allowed fans to buy further in advance and guarantee they would see a specific team over the finals weekend, were made available.

However, they came at a premium, costing more than £150. Adult tickets are available for tonight's action for £60. Even in the best remaining seats, children's prices are £20.

The sheer size of Allianz Stadium, which is behind only Wembley in terms of capacity in the United Kingdom, is also a factor.

A crowd of 22,734 came close to filling the Bluenergy Stadium to watch Fiji beat Italy in Udine last weekend. Had Ireland's match against Australia been staged at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, a 51,700 attendance would be the maximum possible.

Most of the seats on sale in the middle tier are opposite the gantry from which television cameras capture the main match action, in an apparent attempt to improve the spectacle for viewers at home.

A debrief will be carried out by the Nations Championship organisers – a new, dedicated team made up of staff from Six Nations and Sanzaar unions – before cities are given the chance to bid to host the next tournament in 2028.

Qatar had initially been slated as a potential host for that edition, but instability in the Middle East has made a return to Europe more likely.

Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney said earlier this month that Twickenham could stage the event again, while also name-checking France and Spain, which is ambitious to prove itself as a host having bid for the 2035 Rugby World Cup, as other possible destinations.

Organisers are believed to be open-minded about changes to the staging of a competition still in its infancy.

The possibility of one city hosting the event across several stadiums, with lower-profile matches played in smaller venues is one of the developments being considered.

title: Scotland make 11 changes for Argentina game
article_text:
Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend has made 11 changes to his starting XV for Sunday's Nations Championship closer against Argentina at Twickenham (13:10 GMT).

Only record try-scoring wing Darcy Graham, centre Rory Hutchinson, scrum-half Jamie Dobie and lock Jonny Gray retain their places from last weekend's comprehensive victory against Japan, with Finn Russell back at fly-half and flanker Rory Darge returning from injury and captaining the side.

Blair Kinghorn, Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones and Darcy Graham return to the back line.

Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman and D'arcy Rae make up a new front row, Gregor Brown joins Gray in the second row and Josh Bayliss and Magnus Bradbury complete the back row with Darge.

"There's an opportunity with number eights out of our squad with injury," Townsend said.

"Magnus played well in the summer off the bench and he's trained well. He's come [into the squad] in good condition. I'm sure he knows it's a big opportunity for him ahead of the Six Nations.

"We feel this [centre] combination is similar to Sione [Tuipulotu] and Huw [Jones] in terms of the ball-player and the running lines of Huw outside.

"Rory hasn't had a huge amount of opportunities to play at 12 with Sione playing so many games, so it's great for him and for us to see how he goes there."

Townsend also revealed he considered playing replacement hooker Seb Stephen at number eight for this game.

"We spoke to Glasgow a few weeks ago," Townsend explained. "He came off the bench in the back row in Glasgow's last game.

"We don't think it's right this weekend, but given the quality of our three hookers, Seb probably fits that profile more than the other two. His big strength is his ball carrying. He's obviously a very good hooker, but when we're looking at potential options for the back row, he fits that profile."

The Scots and the Pumas are competing to finish seventh in the tournament.

Townsend's Scotland have won four and lost twice so far, while Felipe Contepomi's Argentina have won twice and lost on four occasions.

Contepomi makes three personnel changes with Rodrigo Isgro taking over from Bautista Delguy on the wing and Faustino Sanchez Valarolo coming in at inside centre for Justo Piccardo, who makes the bench.

Juan Martin Scelzo moves from seven to eight with Joaquin Moro coming in at openside and Facundo Isa dropping out.

"They have changed how they've defended over the last few games," Townsend added.

"They are much more aggressive with their line speed, hitting hard and looking to put bodies into contact. With that, there are threats and opportunities.

"They have always had a really good forward pack and they've got talented, skilful backs. We're expecting a top performance from them."

Scotland: Blair Kinghorn, Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones, Rory Hutchinson, Darcy Graham, Finn Russell, Jamie Dobie; Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman, D'arcy Rae, Gregor Brown, Jonny Gray, Josh Bayliss, Rory Darge (capt), Magnus Bradbury.

Replacements: Seb Stephen, Nathan McBeth, Zander Fagerson, Max Williamson, Liam McConnell, Ollie Leatherbarrow, George Horne, Tom Jordan.

Argentina: Geronimo Prisciantelli, Rodrigo Isgro, Lucio Cinti, Faustino Sanchez Valarolo, Ignacio Mendy, Tomas Albornoz, Gonzalo Garcia; Rodrigo Martinez, Julian Montoya (capt), Francisco Moreno, Guido Petti, Pedro Rubiolo, Juan Martin Gonzalez, Joaquin Moro, Juan Martin Scelzo.

Replacements: Facundo Bosch, Joel Sclavi, Tomas Rapetti, Efrain Elias, Santiago Grondona, Agustin Moyano, Justo Piccardo, Tobias Wade.

title: Familiar faces and surprise chances as Ireland face Wallabies
article_text:
Discussion about how Ireland head coach Andy Farrell would approach Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia was ended emphatically by the team announcement on Wednesday.

While Farrell would have been excused for fielding a rotated side in the wake of last week's bruising victory over world champions South Africa, he instead opted for continuity and is challenging his first-choice line-up to produce another chest-thumping 80-minute display against the Wallabies.

Farrell has made two changes from the side that started Saturday's 20-17 success over the Springboks in Dublin, both of which are enforced.

Jacob Stockdale replaces the ill Mack Hansen on the left wing while in-form back row Nick Timoney is restored at number eight in place of the banned Dan Sheehan.

While Ireland cannot win the inaugural Nations Championship, Farrell has emphasised the importance of Friday in the context of the team's journey to next year's World Cup.

Victory over Australia - who they beat 33-31 in Sydney in July - would be four wins in as many weekends. Do that down under next year and Ireland will find themselves in another World Cup quarter-final.

The six-day turnaround between last week's win over South Africa and Friday's contest with Australia serves as useful preparation for next year's tournament, where Ireland will have six days between their pool games against Portugal and Scotland and potentially a quarter and semi-final, should they reach that stage.

With no six-day turnarounds in the 2027 Six Nations, Farrell is keen to test his side within those parameters before they return to their provinces for a busy festive schedule.

While the World Cup unavoidably edges into view, Ireland's immediate priority is to close out a largely positive 2026 on a winning note.

Sobering defeats by France and New Zealand cast doubts over the squad's trajectory, but last week's narrow win over South Africa served as a reminder that Farrell's side can still mix it with the world's best.

And while slaying the Springboks may have restored hope among fans, senior squad figures have carefully tempered expectations as they attempt to round out the year with a 10th win from 12 Tests.

"If you're winning games by the skin of your teeth and not performing well you don't really gain that belief, but when you're playing well and then start winning well the belief comes and that's something that we certainly gained before the 2023 World Cup," said Tadhg Beirne, who will captain Ireland against Australia in Sheehan's absence.

"But we're building that and we're often talking about that in terms of creating that belief, creating that identity that we want to see of ourselves, but again we're nowhere near where we need to be if we want to be competing to win a World Cup next year.

"I think there's so much more growth but we have to keep delivering in these big games for everyone to feel it and I know how it feels back in 2023 going into that World Cup.

"I think everyone in that squad felt it and I think we're certainly on the way there and if we can keep performing the way we've been performing but getting better we'll certainly be there by next year."

Friday night is a big opportunity for Stockdale, who was not involved in the wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.

Nearly nine years removed from his star-making performances for Joe Schmidt's Ireland in the 2018 Grand Slam campaign, the 30-year-old Ulster wing is no longer a nailed-on starter.

But having been picked ahead of Tommy O'Brien - who scored two tries in the win over Fiji - Stockdale must seize an opportunity to impress on what will be his first run-out at Twickenham since a try-scoring cameo off the bench in a behind-closed-doors Autumn Nations Cup defeat by England in November 2020.

Stockdale needn't look far for inspiration. Seven of his Ulster team-mates are in the matchday 23. Two of them - Stuart McCloskey and Timoney - have featured in all 12 Tests this year (alongside Beirne), while jet-heeled right winger Robert Baloucoune is enjoying his best run as an international after a couple of tries against South Africa last week.

In January 2016, Stockdale made his Ulster debut under the province's then director of rugby Les Kiss, the man now leading the Wallabies.

The 61-year-old replaced Schmidt following the July leg of the Nations Championship, and while scrutiny on the Queenslander intensified following defeats by England and Scotland, last week's 29-26 victory over Wales has boosted the Wallaby morale as they attempt to snap a six-game losing streak against the Irish.

Kiss, who was Ireland's defence coach during the historic 2009 Grand Slam triumph, has turned heads with his own selection in the number 11 jersey, with former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm earning his Test debut at the age of 28.

Kurtley Beale - who started Australia's last victory over Ireland in June 2018 - is an eye-catching addition to the bench as the 37-year-old closes in on a first Test cap in five years.

With Kalani Thomas earning a first start at scrum-half and a new back-row combination in Tom Hooper, Carlo Tizzano and Rob Valetini, it is an intriguing Wallabies line-up.

But if Ireland can replicate the intensity and edge they showed against South Africa, they may pass Farrell's World Cup rehearsal and ensure they approach the tantalising possibilities of 2027 in buoyant form.

title: Jenkins ready to resume Wales captaincy role
article_text:
Dafydd Jenkins says he feels more ready now to be Wales captain, having been given the honour of leading his country again in the Nations Championship finale against Japan on Saturday.

Regular captain Dewi Lake and deputy Jac Morgan have both dropped down to the bench for the match at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, as head coach Steve Tandy rotates his side for the-ninth place play-off.

It leaves Exeter lock Jenkins, who turns 24 next month, as the natural choice to reclaim the armband - more than two years after he was given a baptism of fire as Warren Gatland's skipper for the 2024 Six Nations.

With Lake and Morgan injured for that tournament - and a number of senior players having retired after the 2023 World Cup - Jenkins endured a tough test, as Wales suffered a clean sweep of Six Nations defeats for the first time since 2003.

"I am definitely a different person," said Jenkins, who at 21 was the second-youngest Wales captain behind Sir Gareth Edwards.

"I was looking back at when I got it the first time, I feel a lot more settled now within the squad.

"To have that experience before puts me in good stead now."

Jenkins will - for now - retake the role for just one match, with Lake and Morgan having led Wales for the past two years.

However, the 6ft 7in (2.01m) Exeter lock has always been a natural leader, claiming the record as the youngest captain in the English Prem at just 19 years and 342 days old in November 2022.

He has followed that up by becoming the Chiefs' permanent skipper for the past few seasons.

"I'm always trying to develop my game and leadership skills," said Jenkins.

"I'm probably not the loudest leader, but I try to lead through my actions and hope boys follow me.

"I love doing it at Exeter, I love putting the jersey on here with Wales, so whatever's best for the team.

"It will be another special occasion for me and my family."

Tandy says that as part of his squad's leadership group, Jenkins was the natural choice to captain the side on Saturday.

"It's massive credit for him, so well-deserved and a great opportunity for him to lead the team," said the Wales head coach.

Jenkins, Morgan and Lake make up that Wales leadership group, along with others including hooker Ryan Elias, wing Josh Adams and scrum-half Tomos Williams.

"I can't take away from the players I have around me and it is a privileged situation as a captain," added Jenkins.

"I'm very lucky to be in a situation where you have people like Josh on the wing, Ryan in the pack and Adam Beard calling line-outs."

Jenkins, who is set to be one of seven Wales players to start all four games this November, has produced a colossal defensive shift across the campaign.

His most effective contribution was the 38 tackles he made in the victory against New Zealand, during a game in which Wales made a team record of 346.

Jenkins' personal tally equalled the men's individual Test record set by France flanker Thierry Dusautoir against New Zealand in the 2007 World Cup quarter-final in Cardiff.

After missing the first half of World Rugby's new competition during the summer through injury, Jenkins has made 77 Nations Championship tackles, the most of any player, without missing one.

When asked about the tackling records, he says it is just part of his job.

"That's exactly it," said Jenkins. "If someone runs into you, you're going to make the tackle.

"If you look at [prop] Gareth Thomas, he's come off the bench [against New Zealand] and made a stupid amount of tackles, 19 in 26 minutes.

"That is ridiculous and if he's on the whole game, he'd probably double mine!

"It was a huge defensive shift from all the boys after we had been clinical in that first half.

"That's something we probably lacked [in the following week's defeat] against Australia, so we are looking to get that back now against Japan."

"I just love Daf's energy," said the former British and Irish Lions defence coach.

"The work he does in the week is phenomenal and he is the ultimate professional.

"There's a lot of skill to his game also, while the power of his mindset is one of the best I've seen.

"You look at the performance he produced against New Zealand, but he found it to go again against Australia. He made a couple of cover tackles against the Wallabies that probably saved us."

Jenkins is hoping Wales can finish off a successful November by making it three victories in four matches.

"It has been one of the most enjoyable campaigns I've been a part of," he said.

"Obviously because we beat the All Blacks, but the group is as tight as it's ever been since I've been here.

"The competition's there, the training standards are a lot higher than previously, so that's a huge positive to grow for the future."

title: RG Snyman in advanced talks with TOP14 club
article_text:
Stade Français are in advanced talks with Leinster lock RG Snyman about ending his seven-year stay in Ireland and moving to the Top 14 to solve one of their problem areas next season.

Leinster bosses have turned to Snyman, 31, who has helped the Springboks win back-to-back World Cup crowns, after missing out on Australian-born French international Emmanuel Meafou.

Stade made a big play for Meafou to add strength to an area that has been lacking since Baptiste Pesenti, who has four Les Bleus caps, departed in the summer for Pau, but he has decided to stay in Toulouse until 2032.

Snyman, who was voted United Rugby Championship player of the year in 2025, joined Munster seven years ago after a stint in Japan with Tochigi Honda Heat and is in his third year with Leinster but is yet to play a game this season.

His move to Dublin was controversial. He had been set to reunite with Johann van Graan at Bath, only to end up signing for Leinster, where he has made over 30 appearances before rupturing knee ligaments against Glasgow Warriors in March.

Stade have been speaking to Snyman, who appears to be very open to a move to the French capital when his contract runs out at the end of the season, and they have been edging closer to agreeing a deal in the last few days.

And he could become the second massive name to arrive at the Stade Jean-Bouin in a matter of days after it was revealed that All Black star Wallace Sititi is expected to swap the Chiefs for Les Soldats Roses late next year after the World Cup in Australia.

Sititi, 24, is expected to sign a two-year deal with Stade, who, after qualifying for the Top 14 play-offs last season, have found this campaign much harder, sitting in ninth place with 19 points from their nine games.

title: Dubai 7s Invitational: What to expect from the five competing teams
article_text:
The International Invitation competition is the highest rank of the competition outside of the SVNS circuit.

In past years, it’s been a heavily stacked competition, with national sides getting in some reps ahead of the season and charity assembly teams testing their mettle against the best.

This year’s competition looks a little different. The 2025 competition had two pools of five, producing a leaderboard that went on to a knockout finals stage at the iconic Dubai 7s stadium.

This year, with the introduction of the SVNS 3, many of those International Invitational sides have moved into the expanded SVNS set-up. But the Invitational remains high quality.

Ireland, Brazil, Belgium and Hammerheads all return this year to the International Invitational, with 7s up-and-comers Germany looking to make an impact too.

Hammerheads are the last assembly team standing. A privately run, sponsorship-backed team by Leiden Contractors, born from Head Coach Jim Osborne, Hammerheads are an iconic staple of the UK 7s circuit turned international touring team.

In a landscape where opportunities for female players to gain top-level minutes outside of international training camps are still frighteningly small, Hammerheads are bringing a stacked team of international talent to this Dubai 7s.

The squad almost mirrors an Ultimate 7s team, hosting players of eight nationalities including USA flyer Nia Toliver and GB sevens stalwart Isla Norman-Bell, as well as New Zealand up-and-comer Manawa Rogers.

Speaking to Jim Osborne on the eve of the tournament, he reflected on entering this year’s comp as the only non-International side. He said, “It’s so hard because we’ve come out here and half of the people have never met each other, and we’ve just had to go and bond.

“We’ve got two training sessions, one today and one tomorrow, which are basically team runs. We trained at the water park today, doing set pieces, so saving a bit of time so that we don’t have to do that at the next training session.

“We started as a men’s team and brought in the women’s, but the women’s is actually what’s given us our name. Our bread and butter is the women’s side. We get messages all the time from people who want to play, and it’s just an amazing pathway for people to take the next step.

“Ireland will be the biggest challenge. And then Brazil. And then you never know what you’re going to get with Germany and Belgium.

“My dream was to win the Open, which we did four or five years ago. And so it moved from winning the Open to the fairytale ending of winning the Elite.

“Our first game is on pitch 1 against Ireland. It’s going to be unreal.”

Germany are fast becoming one of the most promising sides on the sevens circuit. In front of a strong home crowd at Hamburg at the Europeans in July, they managed a best-place finish at 4th, losing to Spain in the bronze playoff.

They take a strong squad, with no new faces on the teamsheet from their last 7s outing at Split. Mette Zimmat, Paula Schult, and Charlotte Malaizier all featured in Ultimate 7s, with Germany head coach Curtis Bradford gaining some reps too, now bound for the desert this weekend.

They always look like the team to beat. Whether they succeed in those performances against a class of competition will be the biggest test for them.

Belgium have been the underdogs of the European Sevens circuit. They earned a bronze at the European 7s Championship in July in Hamburg, and since their programme went full-time, they’ve developed in style and confidence and look organised.

Their squad for Dubai remains largely unchanged from the summer European Championships.

Lisa Goosens, Romaine Yserbyt, and Lili-Rose Scoriel all return, as well as Abigael Bokonda, who scored the bronze-winning try in Hamburg.

Violette Vekemans, Louka Blommaert and Lea Poucet are new faces in the squad for Dubai. Head coach Terry Bouhraoua will want to gain wins against fellow European teams Belgium, Germany and Ireland.

Known as the ‘Yaras’, they are the only non-European international side in this year’s competition.

Playing in SVNS 2, they’ll be a tough team to beat, bringing an experienced squad. Thalia Costa ran out for Sol Feroz in Ultimate 7s, whilst Isadora Lopes and Gabriela Lima helped bag Pacific Current the inaugural title, Lima scoring a try in the final, not only putting herself but the Brazilian rugby firmly on the map.

They are experienced, and they will be well drilled, confident and, best of all, exciting to watch.

And lastly, Ireland are taking an unbelievably stacked side this tournament. Six Nations fans will recognise members of the ‘Green Wave’ Anna McGann, Stacey Flood, and Eve Higgins, but there is pace across the board as sevens flyers Alana McInerney, Emily Lane and Kathy Baker bolster the squad. Twenty-year-old Leah Irwin earns a call-up after rising through the Ireland U21 programme with strong performances in Ulster and Enniskillen this season.

Having won the second leg of the European Sevens Championship in Split in July, where they beat Poland 26-12, they surely enter the competition as the heavily tipped favourites.
